On what the light is, opinions differ: al-Hasan and Qatada say it is the Qur'an and Islam, al-Kalbi the Qur'an alone, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi take it to be the clear proofs of God's unity and of Muhammad's prophethood. Some read the perfecting of the light as the exaltation of monotheism and the strengthening of Islam, others as the manifestation of the religion. Grammarians also debated the construction in which 'refuse' is followed by 'except': al-Farra' saw an element of negation in it, al-Zamakhshari treated 'refuse' as equivalent to 'does not will', and al-Zajjaj posited an omitted object. These discussions do not change the central message, a promise that the truth will prevail.

God states that He is the One who sent His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ with guidance, meaning the Qur'an and clear explanation, and with the religion of truth, Islam, so that He may make it prevail over all other religions, even if the polytheists dislike it. The commentators agree that the verse contains a promise of the victory and dominance of Islam. They differ, however, on what this

God addresses the believers, warning them against many Jewish rabbis and Christian monks who consume people's wealth unjustly and turn them from God's way, and the commentators also include those who hoard gold and silver without spending it in God's cause. All agree that 'consuming' means 'taking', and that 'unjustly' covers bribery in judgments, distortion of scripture, and selling religious illusions to the common people. Turning from God's way means preventing people from entering Islam or diverting them from the truth. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the rabbis as Jewish scholars and the monks as Christian devotees. On the meaning of hoarding, opinions differ: Ibn Umar, al-Shafi'i, al-Tabari and most scholars say it is wealth whose zakat is not paid, even if buried, while wealth whose zakat is paid is not hoarding even beneath seven earths. Ali ibn Abi Talib holds that anything above four thousand dirhams is hoarding, and Abu Dharr that any surplus beyond need is hoarding. Some companions restricted the verse to the People of the Book, while Abu Dharr and others extended it to Muslims, and Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi read it as general. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the pronoun in 'they do not spend it' refers to gold and silver together or to the wealth. The punishment of branding with heated plates in hell applies to those who withhold what is due, as the authentic hadith reports. All agree that the word 'announce' here is ironic.

This verse warns that those who hoard gold and silver without spending them in the way of God will be given news of a painful punishment: their hoarded wealth will be heated in the fire of Hell and used to brand their foreheads, sides and backs, and they will be told in rebuke that this is what they stored up for themselves, so taste what you used to hoard. The commentators agree on this basic meaning but differ on what counts as hoarding. Al-Tabari, al-Shafi'i and Ibn 'Umar, as cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, hold that any wealth on which zakat is due but not paid is a hoard, whether buried or visible, a view that Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari also report. Ali ibn Abi Talib sets the threshold at four thousand dirhams, whether or not zakat has been paid on it, while Abu Dhar and those with him consider any surplus beyond need to be a hoard. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz considers the verse abrogated by the verse on zakat, whereas most scholars regard it as still valid. On why these three parts of the body are singled out, Abu Bakr al-Warraq explains that the rich man turns his face, side and back away from the poor, and others add that these are the most visible and vital parts. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi list several further reasons, and the commentators also discuss the mode of branding, the reading variants and the traditions attributed to the Prophet on this subject.

This verse states that the number of months with God is twelve, as written in the Preserved Tablet since the day He created the heavens and the earth, and that four of them are sacred: Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, al-Muharram and Rajab. The commentators agree on these names, relying on the Prophet's sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that their sanctity means that violating what is forbidden in them is graver, while al-Mawardi sees the wisdom as training the soul to refrain from sin in them so that it can then refrain in the other months. As for the pronoun 'in them', opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari take it to refer to all twelve months, whereas Qatada, al-Farra' and al-Razi, followed by most scholars, take it to refer to the sacred months alone, where the prohibition of wrongdoing is stronger without being limited to them. The 'wrong' is understood by some as sins, by others as raids and fighting, and by others as the nasi', the pre-Islamic practice of shifting the sanctity from one month to another. On whether the ban on fighting in these months was abrogated, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Zuhri and Qatada hold that it was, while Ata' ibn Abi Rabah holds that it remains except in self-defence. The command to fight the polytheists 'all together' is taken by most as a call to unity, and the promise that God is with the God-fearing as a support granted to those who are conscious of Him.

In this verse God explains that postponing the sacredness of one sacred month to another, which the Arabs called al-nasi', is an increase in their disbelief. They declared a sacred month lawful one year and made it unlawful the next, so as to match the number of the four sacred months God had fixed, and thus they made lawful what God had forbidden. Satan made this evil deed seem fair to them, and God does not guide the disbelieving people. The commentators agree that al-nasi' meant shifting the sanctity of one month to another, a practice used when the Arabs needed raids and fighting, since it was hard for them to endure three consecutive sacred months without raiding. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada report that Junada ibn Awf al-Kinani would proclaim at the pilgrimage that a sacred month was lawful that year, and this recurred until the sanctity circled the whole year. Abu Bakr's pilgrimage fell in Dhu al-Qa'da and the Prophet's in Dhu al-Hijja, hence his words that time had returned to its form on the day God created the heavens and the earth. Accounts differ on who first instituted al-nasi': Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatada name the Banu Malik ibn Kinana, al-Kalbi names Nu'aym ibn Tha'laba, and others mention al-Qalammas. The readings of the verb yudallu also differ: the Medinan, Basran and Syrian readers read yudillu, while the Kufans read yuddallu, and al-Tabari considered both close in meaning. The commentators note that the reproach concerns disregarding the naming of each sacred month, since the Arabs kept only the count.

This verse rebukes believers who dragged their feet when called to set out for the expedition of Tabuk, in the scorching heat, when the dates were ripening and the shade was pleasant, and when resources were scarce. The commentators explain that « ithaqaltum ila al-ard » means that you grew heavy, delayed, and clung to the comfort of home and land. The question « Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter? » is a reproach: how can anyone prefer the pleasures of this world to those of the next, when worldly enjoyment is so small. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj link this reluctance to the season, the ripening of the palms and the love of shade, while al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir stress the hardship of the journey, its great distance and the strength of the enemy. Al-Mawardi offers three readings of « the earth »: attachment to home, to the harvest, or to worldly ease, the last being the view of al-Dahhak. The threat « If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment » is understood by al-Baghawi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as drought in this world, following a report from Ibn Abbas, whereas Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take it more broadly as covering both worlds. For « He will replace you with another people », the commentators name various groups, such as the people of Yemen or the sons of Persia according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr. On abrogation, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Hasan hold that this verse was abrogated by « The believers should not all go forth together », while al-Tabari answers that the obligation applied only to those whom the Prophet called out specifically. Al-Razi concludes that striving is obligatory in general, and most scholars treat it as a collective duty.

This verse warns believers who hold back from going out to fight when the Prophet ﷺ calls them that if they refuse, God will punish them with a painful torment and bring in another people in their place, while their refusal will harm nothing, since God is capable of all things. It was revealed concerning the expedition to Tabuk, undertaken in scorching heat, at harvest time, under hardship, which caused some people to hang back. The commentators differ on the 'painful torment.' Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, took it to mean the withholding of rain from a tribe that had failed to answer the Prophet's call; al-Mawardi also mentions defeat at the hands of enemies, al-Baghawi mentions punishment in the Hereafter or drought in this world, and al-Razi holds that the threat may include both. As for the pronoun in 'they will not harm Him,' al-Hasan, al-Zamakhshari, al-Zajjaj and al-Nasafi take it to refer to God, meaning they will not harm His religion, while most commentators, including al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, take it to refer to the Prophet, whom God had promised protection and victory. The commentators also disagree about the replacement people: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the sons of Persia, Abu Rawq says the people of Yemen, but al-Razi and al-Tabari argue the verse should not be restricted to any particular people. Al-Hasan and Ikrima consider the verse abrogated by 'It is not for the believers to go forth all together'; al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu al-Su'ud reply that there is no abrogation, since it addresses those whom the Prophet summoned and who did not respond, and both verses retain their force.

This verse reminds the believers that God granted victory to His Messenger ﷺ when the disbelievers of Mecca forced him out, when he had only Abu Bakr with him. The commentators explain that it is an argument to urge the faithful to support him: if they refuse to march out, God will still give him victory, as He did in that extreme moment when he had just one companion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the cave is the cave of Thawr, where the two men stayed three days. They all relate the Prophet's words to Abu Bakr, 'Do not grieve, God is with us', and note that Abu Bakr's anxiety came from fear for the Prophet's safety rather than cowardice. Opinions differ on who 'his tranquillity' refers to: the majority, including Ibn Abbas, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir, take it to be the Prophet, while al-Razi and Ibn Attiya report that some read it as referring to Abu Bakr, who was the more distressed. For the 'hosts you did not see', most commentators identify them as the angels of Badr and other battles, while al-Baghawi also mentions angels who turned the enemies' eyes away. On 'the word of those who disbelieved was made lowest', Ibn Abbas understands it as polytheism and God's word as the testimony of faith. The accounts of the cave, such as the pigeons' nest and the spider's web, are cited by several authors, including al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, though not all accept them as sound. Many scholars also cite this verse as evidence of Abu Bakr's high rank.

God commands the believers to set out for the cause of God, whether light or burdened, and to strive with their wealth and their persons, saying that this is better for them if they know it. Commentators differ widely on the meaning of 'light and heavy'. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrima, Abu Salih and Muqatil ibn Hayyan take it to mean young and old, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada mean eager or unwilling, al-Hakam means the busy and the free, Ibn Zayd and Abu Salih mean the wealthy and the poor or those with property and those without, and al-Awza'i means riders and foot soldiers. Murra al-Hamdani speaks of the healthy and the sick, and al-Mawardi of being quick to obey and slow to disobey. Al-Tabari, whose view is the one he prefers, holds that the verse covers everyone, strong or weak, and several companions such as Abu Talha, Abu Ayyub, Safwan ibn 'Amr, al-Miqdad and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab are reported to have gone out despite their frailty. Many place its revelation in the expedition of Tabuk. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and others consider it abrogated by verses granting excuses, whereas al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur hold it unabrogated and say the obligation becomes individual when the enemy attacks and collective otherwise. As for striving with wealth and person, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir treat it as an obligation according to one's ability, and whoever cannot fight should help with his money. Some explain that 'better for you' means better than the rest and comfort one would seek by staying behind.

This verse describes the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk. Had what they were called to been a near gain and an easy, moderate journey, they would have followed the Prophet ﷺ. But the long and hard distance weighed on them, so when he returns they will swear by God that they would have gone out with him had they been able. In doing so they destroy themselves, and God knows that they are liars. The commentators agree that the verse concerns these hypocrites who stayed behind at Tabuk. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that 'a near gain' refers to worldly benefit, meaning booty, and that 'the distance' is the long, exhausting journey. The oath concerns a future event after the return, which several, including al-Razi, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi, present as evidence of prophethood. On the meaning of 'they destroy themselves', al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read it as ruin caused by the false oath and the lie, while al-Mawardi also allows that it means remaining behind. Al-Razi notes that a false oath brings ruin and cites a hadith about the perjurous oath. On ability, al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari distinguish material means from physical strength, and al-Razi reports a debate between the Mu'tazilites and those who hold that ability precedes the act. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Wahidi state that these men were in fact able to go. The commentaries do not name specific individuals, and the reproach addresses the group of hypocrites as a whole.

In this verse God addresses a rebuke to His Prophet ﷺ after opening with pardon as a gesture of kindness. He asks why he granted leave to the hypocrites to stay behind from the Tabuk expedition, and notes that it would have been better to wait until those with genuine excuses were distinguished from the liars. The commentators broadly agree on the general sense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as a reproach for leaving the better course, since the Prophet had granted permission on his own judgement without a divine command. They report, through Amr ibn Maymun and Qatada, that the Prophet did two things without being commanded: this permission and taking ransom from the prisoners of Badr. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the pardon as a metonymy for a fault, whereas al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold that the question is a statement of fact rather than a censure, and place the verse within the realm of the preferable. Ibn Abbas says the Prophet did not yet know the hypocrites at that time. According to Qatada, a verse in Surat al-Nur abrogated or relaxed this ruling, while Ibn Atiyya rejects this on the ground that the two verses were revealed at different times. Sufyan ibn Uyayna and others see in opening with pardon a gentle courtesy toward the Prophet. Opinions also differ on what the permission concerned: remaining behind, according to the majority, or departing, according to a view al-Razi attributes to Abu Muslim. Al-Razi draws from the verse the obligation of caution and deliberation before judging, and the permissibility of personal reasoning for prophets.

This verse teaches that sincere believers do not ask the Prophet for permission to stay behind from fighting, whether with their wealth or their persons. Most commentators agree that someone who asks to remain behind without a valid excuse is a hypocrite who does not believe in God and the Last Day. The verse belongs to the context of the expedition to Tabuk. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that asking to stay back is a sign of hypocrisy, and Ibn Kathir adds that believers see jihad as an act of devotion and hasten to it. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the most faithful Emigrants and Helpers used to say they would never ask the Prophet for leave. Exegetes and grammarians differ on the phrase 'an yujahidu': some treat it as an object after a dropped preposition, others read it as meaning 'out of dislike of fighting'. Al-Razi devotes a long discussion to the verse, raising the question of whether doubt in one point undermines faith, and answers that a believer may doubt one matter without losing his faith as a whole. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi note that the closing phrase, 'God knows the God-fearing', both testifies to the piety of the believers and promises them a great reward. Most commentators agree that the verse separates believers from hypocrites, and that God knows the truly pious.

This verse states that those who ask the Prophet ﷺ for permission to stay behind from fighting are those who do not believe in God or the Last Day, whose hearts are in doubt, and who waver in their uncertainty. The commentators identify these people as the hypocrites, whom some reports number at thirty-nine men. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the doubt (rayb) as uncertainty and bewilderment, and describe the wavering as a man who steps forward with one foot and draws back with the other. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that these men were not sincere seekers of truth but swung between the two sides. Al-Razi distinguishes knowledge, ignorance, supposition and doubt, and explains that doubt settles in the heart. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report that several scholars considered this verse abrogated by the verse in Surat al-Nur beginning "The believers are only those who believe in God and His Messenger"; Ibn 'Atiyya rejects this view as a mistake, while Ibn al-Jawzi argues that abrogation is not required because both verses can be applied together. The commentators also recount the occasion of revelation during the expedition to Tabuk and the rebuke to the Prophet for granting permission before the truth of the claims was clear, which Ibn 'Ashur links to doubt about the outcome of the campaign. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi emphasise that faith in God and the Last Day is what drives a believer to fight. All agree that sincere believers do not seek exemption but hasten to fight when called.

This verse concerns the hypocrites who asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to stay behind from the expedition to Tabuk. It shows that their readiness was not genuine: had they really wanted to go, they would have prepared provisions, mounts and weapons. Allah disliked their setting out and held them back, and it was said to them: sit with those who sit. The commentators agree that the 'provision' means what a traveller and fighter needs, and that 'sitting' means staying behind. On who spoke these words, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir report that the notables spoke among themselves; Ibn Abbas and Muqatil take it as a divine abandonment inspired in their hearts; al-Baghawi, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi add that the Prophet himself may have said it in anger, a view also recorded by al-Razi. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also mention the whisperings of Satan. Nearly all explain God's displeasure by the harm their departure would have caused, namely disorder, discord and spying, as the following verse makes clear. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi note that the hypocrites' doubt was a constant wavering rather than a sincere search for truth. On the Prophet's permission and the rebuke that followed, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud link it to a decision taken before the sincere were distinguished from the liars, while al-Shawkani notes that others see it as a mere opening formula.

This verse explains why God disliked the hypocrites setting out with the believers on the expedition to Tabuk. The commentators agree that their going out would have brought only corruption, confusion and poor judgment to the Muslims. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the verb awda'a means to hasten, so the phrase describes them rushing between the ranks to spread slander and incitement. Most commentators understand the discord as dividing the community, though al-Dahhak and Muqatil take fitna to mean disbelief, while al-Hasan reads it as splitting the word and al-Kalbi as blame and evil. On the phrase about those among you who listen to them, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Kalbi take it to mean spies who carry news to the hypocrites, whereas al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim hold that it means people who listen to them and obey them, a view Ibn al-Qayyim finds stronger. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya discuss whether the exception clause is continuous or discontinuous, with both readings reported. The verse ends by affirming that God knows the wrongdoers fully, which covers both those who stayed behind and those who listened to them.

This verse states that the hypocrites sought to sow discord among the believers and split their ranks even before the expedition to Tabuk, and that they turned affairs against the Prophet ﷺ through schemes, until the truth came, God's command prevailed, and they were unwilling. The commentators agree that fitna means discord that breaks unity, and that turning over affairs means scheming and examining every side of a matter. They differ, however, on which earlier episodes are meant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya mainly point to the withdrawal of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy with his men at Uhud, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir also cite Ibn Jurayj's report that twelve hypocrites waited at the Thaniyyat al-Wada' on the night of 'Aqaba to assassinate the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Wahidi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi place these acts before Tabuk or during it. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi offer several readings of the phrase: an outward show of help together with secret alliance with the polytheists, speaking with the tongue what is not in the heart, or waiting for misfortune. Regarding the occasion of revelation, most reports cited by al-Tabari concern Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Ibn Nabtal, Rifa'a and Zayd ibn al-Tabut. As for the 'truth' that came, some understand it as help and victory, others as the Qur'an and the Prophet's mission.

This verse reports that some hypocrites asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to stay behind from the expedition to Tabuk, saying: grant me leave and do not put me to trial. The commentators explain that the trial meant may be the temptation of women or the sin of disobedience. Most, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir citing Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, report that the verse was revealed about Jadd ibn Qays, who claimed he was strongly drawn to women and feared he could not resist the women of the Byzantines. Qatada, followed by al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi in one opinion, took the trial to mean sin, while al-Mawardi also gave the meanings of ruin and punishment.

The phrase they have fallen into the very trial they sought to avoid is understood by most as meaning that they fell into the trial of desertion and hypocrisy. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi stress this reading, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the verb suggests a sudden and complete fall. As for Hell encompassing the disbelievers, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi relate it to the Day of Resurrection, whereas al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud also see it as already present, since its causes surround them now.

Modern commentators such as Sayyid Qutb and Ibn 'Ashur emphasise the vividness of the image and the irony of men who fled a trial only to fall into a greater one. Ibn Sa'di adds that desertion is a far greater harm than the danger they feared.

This verse describes the attitude of the hypocrites towards the Prophet ﷺ and the believers: when good fortune reaches them, it distresses them, and when a misfortune strikes, they say they had already taken their precaution by staying behind, and then they turn away, rejoicing. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, as cited by al-Tabari, understand the good as victory and booty and the misfortune as defeat. Al-Mawardi, al-Kalbi and al-Sam'ani report that the good refers to the victory at Badr and the misfortune to the setback at Uhud, while Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Qasimi hold that the wording is general and the examples are illustrative. On the phrase about having taken their precaution, Mujahid reads it as caution, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi as vigilance and firmness, and Ibn 'Atiyya as a claim of prudence in holding back. As for turning away, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as apostasy or abandoning the Prophet, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it as leaving their gathering where they boast together. Several commentators, including Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Ashur, link the passage to the expedition of Tabuk and to Jadd ibn Qays, whose account is reported by Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that some versions of that account are weak. The reply in the following verse, that only what God has decreed will reach the believers and that He is their protector, is explained by al-Razi and the Jalalayn.

This verse records the Prophet's reply to the hypocrites who rejoiced at having stayed behind from the expedition: when good befalls the believers it grieves them, and when a misfortune strikes they say they had taken their precaution in advance. The plain meaning, as most commentators explain it, is that nothing will touch the believers except what God has decreed and written for them, that He is their protector and helper, and that the believers should place their trust in Him alone. The exegetes agree that the answer is both a rebuke to the hypocrites and a comfort to the Prophet and the believers, and that it implies acceptance of God's decree. They differ on the meaning of "what God has written for us". Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars, including al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir, take it as what God has decreed or recorded in the Preserved Tablet. Al-Zajjaj, followed by Ibn al-Jawzi, understands it as what God has promised in His Books, namely victory or martyrdom, both good outcomes for the believer. Al-Mawardi takes it as the victory promised in the final outcome. Al-Razi holds that everything is decreed and that the decree cannot change, while al-Shawkani and al-Alusi stress God's determination and choice. According to Ibn 'Abbas the good refers to the battle of Badr and the misfortune to Uhud, but al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider the wording general, the context concerning the expedition. On recitation, Ibn Mas'ud and Talha ibn Musarrif read "hal yusibuna", and the emphatic nun after "lan" attributed to A'yan is judged faulty by Abu Hatim and most commentators. All agree that trust in God means entrusting one's affair to Him while still taking the means, and that the believers in battle gain one of the two excellent outcomes, victory or martyrdom.

The verse tells the Prophet to answer the hypocrites who wait for misfortune to strike the believers: you await for us only one of the two good outcomes, victory with spoils or martyrdom, and both are good for the believers. For our part, we await for you that God strike you with a punishment from Him, such as a calamity from heaven or destruction like that of earlier nations, or that He permit us to fight you. The commentators read these words as a threat and a warning: let them wait, for the believers are also waiting to see their own end. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada agree that the two good outcomes are victory or martyrdom, that the punishment from God means lightning, a calamity or death, and that the punishment by the believers' hands means killing. Al-Wahidi and al-Sam'ani cite a hadith in which God guarantees the fighter either paradise or his return home with his reward. Al-Razi notes that the believer wins either way, while the hypocrite loses either way. Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take the imperative as a threat rather than a command. Al-Hasan explains that the hypocrites' waiting is for the promises of Satan, and the believers' waiting for the promises of God. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note differences in recitation that do not change the meaning. Ibn Kathir concludes that the believers attain one of the two good outcomes, while the hypocrites face one of the two bad ones.

In this verse God tells His Prophet to say to the hypocrites: spend, whether willingly or under compulsion, but it will not be accepted from you, because you were a defiantly disobedient people, meaning people who had departed from faith and obedience to God. Most commentators read the imperative as carrying the sense of a condition or of a statement: whatever way they spend, their money is not accepted, as al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain. Many report that the verse was revealed about Jadd ibn Qays, who asked to stay behind from the expedition to Tabuk and offered to help with his wealth instead; al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir mention this, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the ruling was general afterwards. The meaning of willingly and under compulsion is explained in different ways: al-Razi and al-Nasafi take compulsion to be the obligation imposed by the Prophet, which the hypocrites found burdensome, while al-Zamakhshari suggests the pressure of their leaders. As to why it was rejected, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir attribute it to hypocrisy and doubt about the religion, and Ibn Kathir also cites the principle that God accepts only what is good. Al-Razi notes that al-Jubba'i drew from the verse that sinfulness cancels good deeds, but he replies that the only barrier is disbelief, as the following verse shows, which also mentions laziness in prayer and reluctance to give. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the word for perverse refers here to unbelievers who hide their disbelief. Al-Sa'di concludes that deeds are accepted only from believers, and that one should give with a glad heart, hoping for reward from God alone. Differences in readings and grammar have little effect on the central meaning.

This verse explains why the hypocrites' expenditures are not accepted. The commentators agree that the main reason is their disbelief in Allah and His Messenger, while their apparent acts, such as prayer and spending, do not come from sincere intention. They pray lazily because they hope for no reward and fear no punishment for neglecting it, and they spend unwillingly because they regard spending as a loss rather than a gain. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi see disbelief as the cause that prevents acceptance, with laziness and reluctance as its signs. Ibn Kathir adds that deeds are valid only through faith. Al-Razi discusses whether disbelief alone produces the result or whether the three factors act together, and concludes that each is an indicator rather than a decisive cause. Al-Zamakhshari notes that laziness is a trait of the hypocrites that a believer must avoid. The readers differ between the forms 'tuqbala' and 'yuqbala', with Hamza and al-Kisa'i using the yā' because the feminine of 'expenditures' is not real. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the word 'willingly' in the previous verse does not contradict 'unwillingly' here: their giving is not ordered by the Prophet or their leaders, and it does not stem from genuine desire. Ibn Sa'di stresses that every act requires faith, and that the believer should pray eagerly and give with an open heart. Ibn 'Atiyya concludes that, in essence, these people pray and spend out of fear rather than to draw near to Allah.

God addresses His Prophet ﷺ: do not be impressed by the wealth and children of these hypocrites, for God intends to punish them through them in this worldly life, and for their souls to depart while they are disbelievers. Commentators differ on the nature of this punishment. Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas, followed by Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Qutayba, hold that the verse has an inversion: the meaning is that their wealth should not impress in this world, and the punishment through it will come in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan al-Basri, whom al-Tabari chose and Ibn Kathir called the strongest view, explains that the punishment is the zakat taken from them and their spending in God's way, given unwillingly. Ibn Zayd understands the misfortunes that befall their wealth and children, which are a punishment for them and a reward for believers. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and others add the hardship of acquiring and guarding wealth, the fear of losing it, and the grief of separation. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read the divine will as a respite that lets the hypocrites die heedless, a reading that al-Alusi discusses in terms of divine will and that rests on the same grammatical question. Most commentators agree that dying in disbelief is a clear statement. Al-Razi notes that hypocrisy brings every harm in this life and the next, and Ibn al-Qayyim develops at length the suffering that attachment to the world causes.

This verse reports that the hypocrites swear by God that they belong to the believers, while in truth they do not belong to them inwardly, and fear is what drives them to this oath. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand this fear as dread of being killed or of suffering what is done to the polytheists, so they show Islam out of prudence (taqiyya). Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi keep the same sense, adding that they fear being treated like the idolaters. Al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi simply explain that the word farq means fear. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the verse speaks of the group as a whole rather than naming individuals. For what follows, most commentators explain that if they found a refuge, a cave or an underground passage, they would rush into it. The word malja' is taken as a fortress or a safe place, the maghārāt as caves in the mountains, and the mudkhal as a tunnel or underground shaft. The readings of the word mudkhalan vary, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that yajmahūn means to advance without being checked. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the wording shows the hypocrites are disbelievers at heart and that their fear is what leads them to feign faith. Al-Sha'rawi sees in the oath an inner contradiction in these men. The commentators present these different readings without choosing between them.

This verse describes the hypocrites' cowardice and fear: were they to find a refuge, caves, or a hidden passage in the earth, they would flee there headlong, away from the believers. The commentators largely agree on the meaning of the terms. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain the malja' as a fortress or secure place, the maghârât as caves or hollows in the mountains, and the mudkhal as an underground tunnel where one hides. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi follow these explanations. The verb yajmahun means to rush forward without being restrained, like a skittish horse; al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi cite a line attributed to Muhalhil to illustrate it. Ibn Kathir reads the verse together with the preceding oath, in which the hypocrites swear they belong to the believers out of fear. Other views move away from the literal sense: al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi mention that the refuge may be a group of people who protect them, and the mudkhal a tribe in which they could blend. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di present the verse mainly as a portrait of hearts without courage, unable to stand firm in hardship. Readings also differ, as Ibn 'Ashur notes that maghârât can derive from two roots and mudkhal can be vocalised in several ways, though the general idea of flight remains the same.

This verse describes hypocrites who criticise the Prophet ﷺ over the distribution of charity: if they receive a share they are pleased, and if they do not they become angry. Al-Tabari explains that their criticism does not stem from religion but from their own interests, and Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di likewise hold that their contentment and anger follow their worldly desires alone. Most commentators understand the verb lamaza as blaming or defaming, while Mujahid gives it the sense of testing or pressing for gifts, and al-Kalbi renders it as reproach. Nearly all report that the revelation followed a challenge to the Prophet during a distribution. They differ, however, on who made it: al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir name Dhu al-Khuwayswira al-Tamimi, who asked him to be just, while al-Kalbi, al-Baydawi and al-Suyuti mention Abu al-Jawwaz, and al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi mention Tha'laba ibn Hatib. Ibn 'Ashur links the behaviour to the stinginess characteristic of hypocrites. Al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and others stress that the purpose is to expose the baseness of such people and to call for contentment, which the following verses set against their attitude by describing what Allah and His Messenger give.

This verse describes hypocrites who criticize the Prophet ﷺ over the distribution of charity and accuse him of unfairness: when they receive something they are pleased, and when they receive nothing they become angry. God then shows what would have been better for them: to be content with what God and His Messenger gave them, to say "God is sufficient for us," to hope for God's bounty and that of His Messenger, and to turn to God alone. The commentators agree that the answer to "if" (law) is omitted, meaning "it would have been better for them." Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the critic was Tha'laba ibn Hatib, or Dhu al-Khuwaysira, or Abu al-Jawwas, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Sa'id about Dhu al-Khuwaysira. Al-Tabari adds that gifts were given to the people of Mecca to win their hearts. Al-Razi draws the lesson that whoever seeks worldly gain may end in hypocrisy, and distinguishes four levels of contentment: accepting God's decree, voicing it, hoping for His favour, and turning to Him alone. Ibn Ashur explains that "what God gave them" refers to the charity God assigned to those categories. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya focus on the hypocrites' fault, while the commentators do not decide who the precise critic was. They all agree on the lesson of trust in God and turning to Him alone.

This verse specifies the recipients of the obligatory alms, limited to the eight categories it names and not extended beyond them. The commentators agree that the faqir and the miskin are two categories joined by need, but they differ on which is worse off. Al-Asma'i, Yunus ibn Habib and others hold that the faqir is better off than the miskin, while al-Shafi'i holds the reverse. Al-Tabari reports that the faqir is one in need who refrains from asking, and the miskin one who asks and abases himself, while Qatada defines the faqir as the disabled needy person and the miskin as the able-bodied needy one. The collectors ('amilun) are paid according to their work and the customary wage, according to Ibn 'Umar, Malik and Abu Hanifa, while Mujahid and al-Dahhak say they receive one eighth. Those whose hearts are to be reconciled were people the Prophet won over with gifts; 'Umar and several others held that their share ended once Islam became strong, while al-Zuhri and Ahmad held that it remains when needed. For the freeing of slaves, most jurists understand the mukatabun, slaves contracted to buy their freedom, while Ibn 'Abbas allowed outright manumission. The debtors (gharimun) are those who incurred debt for a lawful cause. Fighters in the path of God receive a share, with disagreement over whether the wealthy among them qualify, and some extend it to pilgrimage. The wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) receives enough to return home even if wealthy where he is. On distribution, al-Shafi'i requires sharing among all eight categories, whereas Umar, Huzayfa, Ibn 'Abbas, Malik and Abu Hanifa allow giving to a single category, treating the verse as defining the destinations rather than mandating equal division. The verse sits within a passage on hypocrites who mocked the Prophet over the distribution of alms, and it affirms that his distribution followed God's command.

This passage addresses a group of hypocrites who harmed the Prophet ﷺ with their words and called him "an ear," meaning one who listens to everything said to him and accepts it. The Quran replies that he is an ear of good for them: he hears what is good, believes in God, trusts the believers, and is a mercy for those among them who had believed. As for those who harm the Messenger of God, a painful punishment awaits them.

The commentators agree that the harm consisted of disparaging the Prophet and passing on his words, and that "udhun" means a listener who accepts whatever he hears. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir report that the speaker was Nabtal ibn al-Harith, while Ibn Ishaq and al-Baghawi also mention Jalas ibn Suwayd, and al-Kalbi and Muqatil link the verse to hypocrites who stayed behind from the Tabuk expedition. The reports of the occasion of revelation vary, and the commentators do not decide between them.

The readings differ. Most read "udhunu khayrin lakum" as an construct phrase, whereas al-Hasan, Mujahid and others read "udhunun khayrun", meaning that listening to them and believing them would be better for them than calling them liars. Al-Tabari prefers the first reading. Hamza reads "wa rahmatin" in the genitive, and the majority in the nominative. Grammarians differ on the lam in "yu'minu lil-mu'minin": some take it as superfluous, others as linked to an implied verbal noun, as al-Mubarrad does. Al-Zamakhshari distinguishes believing in God, which takes "bi", from trusting the believers, which takes "li".

The commentators also stress the Prophet's patience and forbearance, since he did not expose the hypocrites and accepted their excuses, which explains their remark. Ibn Ashur sees the divine reply as a way of turning the sense of the hostile words around. The closing threat is directed at anyone who harms the Messenger, in whatever form the harm takes.

This verse describes the hypocrites who swear oaths by God to the believers in order to win their approval, regarding what had reached them of their insults and harm toward the Prophet ﷺ. It states that God and His Messenger deserve more to be pleased, through repentance, obedience and loyalty, if these people are truly believers. Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report the occasion of revelation: a hypocrite said that if what Muhammad says is true, then his companions are worse than donkeys; a young Ansari, Amir ibn Qays, answered him, and the hypocrites swore falsely that he was lying, so the verse came down. Baghawi and Wahidi also mention a version connected with the expedition to Tabuk, which Razi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur also cite. The commentators agree that these oaths are false, aimed at averting the anger of the believers, and that God's pleasure is gained only through obedience. On the singular pronoun in 'yurdhuhu', Sibawayh, as cited by Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi, takes it as two clauses with the predicate of the first omitted; al-Mubarrad proposes inversion; Zamakhshari and Nasafi hold that the pleasure of God and of the Messenger is one, so one pronoun suffices; Razi gives several reasons, including that only God knows the sincerity of the heart. Sayyid Qutb and Shawkani add that the sincere believer seeks God's pleasure rather than that of people.

This verse rebukes the hypocrites for failing to recognise a plain truth: whoever opposes God and His Messenger and stands against them will have the Fire of Hell as his abode, to remain in it forever, and that is the great disgrace. The commentators explain the word muhadda in different ways. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean opposition, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan describe it as one party standing on a boundary different from that of the other, that is, a clash of positions. Abu Muslim derives it from the edge of weapons and so understands armed hostility. On grammar, the common reading opens the second "anna", which Sibawayh and al-Khalil treat as a substitution for the first, whereas al-Mubarrad and al-Jarmi see it as a repetition for emphasis because the sentence is long. Some hold that the reading with a kasra begins a new clause after the particle fa, and Abu Hayyan considers this reading strong in Arabic. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that khizy can mean remorse or shame, and al-Razi prefers remorse here. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from the verse that one who opposes God and His Messenger has no covenant to protect him. Most commentators connect the verse to the hypocrites who swore falsely to the believers after Tabuk, or who insulted the Prophet.

This verse describes the hypocrites fearing that a surah will be revealed about them, exposing what their hearts conceal. God then tells His Prophet to say: mock as you like, for God will bring out what you fear. The commentators agree that the fear is that their hypocrisy will be exposed, and that the command to mock is a threat. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the surah was called al-Fadiha, the Exposer, because it laid bare their conduct, and Qatada mentions other names it had. The main disagreement concerns the verb 'to fear'. Al-Hasan and Qatada, followed by Ibn al-Jawzi, take it as a statement about their state, while al-Zajjaj reads it as a command meaning 'let them beware'. The pronouns are also debated. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take 'upon them' and 'informs them' to refer to the believers, and 'in their hearts' to the hypocrites, while others refer all of them to the hypocrites. Ibn 'Ashur suggests the fear may be a feigned display of mockery, following Abu Muslim al-Isfahani. On how a disbeliever could fear revelation, al-Razi answers that the hypocrites had seen the Prophet disclose what they hid, or that envy can blind a person to the truth. Several occasions of revelation are reported: remarks made on the march to Tabuk, a plot to attack the Prophet at a steep pass, and a remark by Waddi'a ibn Thabit. Ibn Kathir compares the verse with the surah of Muhammad, where God is said to bring out the hypocrites' spite.

The verse reports that if the Prophet ﷺ questioned the hypocrites about their mocking words, they would reply that they were only chatting and joking on the road to pass the time. God then tells His Prophet to expose them by reminding them that they were mocking God, His signs and His messenger, and to ignore their excuse. The commentators link the passage to the expedition of Tabuk, when some people said that the reciters of the Quran were greedier in their bellies, more lying in their tongues and more cowardly in battle, or spoke about conquering the palaces of Syria. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report that the speaker was Wadi'a ibn Thabit, while Ibn Ishaq and others also name Makhshi ibn Humayyar. Al-Tabari transmits a report that the man clinging to the camel's strap was Abdullah ibn Ubayy, but Ibn Atiyya rejects this because he did not attend Tabuk. The exegetes agree that mocking God, His signs or His messenger is disbelief, and that a false excuse is useless once disbelief has been revealed; al-Qurtubi notes that joking about disbelief is still disbelief. On the division between a pardoned group and a punished group, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the pardoned person is one man who repented, while others speak of three men, one of whom, who did not mock, was pardoned. Al-Razi holds that the laugher committed a lighter offence than the mockers, and Ibn Kathir stresses that repentance removes the punishment. The overall meaning retained is that a hypocrite cannot clear himself with a lie, and that mocking religion is disbelief which brings punishment if its perpetrator persists in it.

This verse tells the hypocrites not to offer excuses, because they have disbelieved after professing faith, by mocking Allah, His signs and His messenger. It adds that if Allah pardons one group among them, He will punish another group for their persistent crimes. The commentators agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the mockery was aimed at the Prophet and the Quran, and that their excuse was that they were only chatting and joking. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and others hold that the pardoned person was a single man, Makhshi ibn Humayr al-Ash'ari, and that the word "group" here refers to one individual, a usage supported by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Ibn Ishaq and al-Baghawi add that he repented and was later killed as a martyr at al-Yamama. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand the pardon as applying to those who repent or refrain from harming the Prophet, and the punishment to those who persist in hypocrisy.

Scholars differ on the phrase "you have disbelieved after your faith", since these men were not truly believers. Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that it means they had openly displayed faith, a view also attributed to al-Hasan, whereas al-Razi holds that real disbelief was committed and renewed. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi state that mocking religion is disbelief, and that jesting and serious speech are equal when they utter words of unbelief, a position al-Alusi also reports.

Al-Qurtubi notes that the root meaning of the word for excuse is effacing the trace of a fault, and that the prohibition stems from the fact that such excuses are plainly false.

This verse states that hypocrites, men and women alike, form a single category: they resemble one another in professing faith with the tongue while concealing disbelief in the heart. The commentators describe their conduct. They enjoin what is reprehensible, which is disbelief and disobedience to God and His Messenger, and forbid what is good, which is faith and obedience. They withhold their hands from spending in God's way. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Juraij take this as refusal to give, while Qatada understands it as withholding from every good. Al-Mawardi also reports the views that it means abstaining from fighting or from raising the hands in supplication.

As for "they forgot God, so He made them forget themselves," most exegetes read forgetting as abandonment: they neglected His obedience, and He withdrew from them His guidance and mercy. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that literal forgetting cannot be attributed to God, so the expression is figurative or a rhetorical response. Qatada holds that the forgetting applies to good and not to evil.

The commentators agree that the hypocrites have departed from obedience to God, and that their wickedness is more severe than that of others, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi observe. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite traditions on the three signs of the hypocrite. Ibn Kathir, relying on Ibn 'Abbas, reports that there were about three hundred men and one hundred and seventy women among them in Medina.

Ibn 'Ashur notes that the mention of women establishes equal judgment for both sexes.

The commentators explain that God has promised the hypocrites, men and women, and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, where they will remain forever. That fire is sufficient for them as a recompense, and God has cursed them, meaning He has removed them far from His mercy, while a lasting torment awaits them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree on the apparent meaning: eternal damnation and banishment from God's mercy. As for the phrase 'it is sufficient for them', al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take it as a sign of the extreme severity of the punishment, which cannot be increased, while Ibn Atiyya says it is a recompense exactly matched to their deeds. Ibn Sa'di explains that the grouping of hypocrites with disbelievers reflects their shared unbelief and hostility toward God and His Messenger. On the 'lasting torment', opinions differ: most place it in the afterlife, and al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud see it as a kind of punishment separate from the fire itself, whereas al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi also read it as the suffering the hypocrites endure in this world, the weariness of hypocrisy and the constant fear of exposure. Ibn Ashur notes that the past tense expresses a firm divine commitment, and that the verse may refer to a punishment in this world, that of shame and humiliation among people.

This verse addresses the hypocrites, telling them that they are following the path of earlier peoples who were stronger and had more wealth and children, and who enjoyed their share of this world. The hypocrites did the same, and then plunged into vain talk as those had done. Their deeds are therefore nullified in this world and the next, and they are the losers. The commentators agree on the addressees and on the general sense of the comparison: the likeness lies in enjoying worldly goods and immersing oneself in falsehood. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada take the word khalaq to mean religion or portion, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as being content with a worldly portion at the expense of the hereafter, and al-Mawardi sees it as pursuing desires or clinging to a creed. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the repetition of enjoyment as a rebuke that prepares the final comparison. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of Abu Hurayra about following the ways of earlier nations, which Ibn 'Atiyya considers ill-suited to this verse. Khawd is explained as lying, mocking the Prophet, or idle play, depending on the commentator. Al-Mawardi suggests the earlier peoples may be the Persians and Romans or the Children of Israel. All agree that the deeds are void of reward and that the loss is in both worlds.

This verse reminds the hypocrites that the accounts of earlier peoples have reached them: the people of Noah, drowned in the flood, 'Ad, destroyed by a fierce wind, Thamud, struck by the cry or the earthquake, the people of Abraham, who lost their blessings and whose king Nimrod perished, the people of Madyan, the folk of Shu'ayb, struck by the punishment of the day of the cloud, and the overturned cities, the towns of Lot's people. Each of these nations received messengers bearing clear proofs, and rejected them. The commentators agree that God did not wrong them: He established the proof against them by sending messengers, and it was they who wronged themselves by exposing themselves to punishment through disbelief and denial. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the address as directed first at the hypocrites of the Prophet's time, some extending it to anyone who follows their path. Ibn 'Atiyya prefers that the pronoun 'their messengers' refers to all these nations, while al-Tabari allows that it may refer only to the people of the overturned cities, each city having had its own messenger. Sources identify the overturned cities with Lot's people but differ on their number: three, four, seven or nine. Some commentators, including al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazilites, stress that God, being wise, never punishes without fault, whereas others simply affirm that the punishment was deserved.

This verse describes the believing men and women in contrast to the hypocrites mentioned just before. It says they are allies of one another, meaning they support, help and love each other. The commentators then explain that they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, establish prayer, give zakat, and obey God and His Messenger, before God promises them His mercy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand wilaya as mutual support, affection and help, while al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi add mutual compassion. Abu al-'Aliya explains enjoining good as calling from polytheism to Islam, and forbidding evil as rejecting the worship of idols and devils, while Ibn 'Abbas says the prayer refers to the five daily prayers. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that praise for voluntary prayers is stronger, since one who maintains them is more likely to keep the obligatory ones, and that the zakat meant is the obligatory one. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi say the sin in "will surely have mercy on them" makes the mercy certain, whereas Abu Hayyan explains that it merely marks the future tense.

On "Mighty, Wise", al-Tabari sees God's power in His vengeance, while Ibn Sa'di describes Him as the one who places everything in its proper place. Several commentators connect the verse to the promise of gardens of Eden and pleasant dwellings. On the meaning of Eden, Ibn Mas'ud takes it as the middle of Paradise, al-Hasan as a palace, al-Dahhak as the city of Paradise, and Ka'b as vineyards in Persian, which Ibn 'Atiyya considers a confusion with Firdaws. The commentators broadly agree that God's good pleasure is greater than all bliss, and that this is the great triumph.

This verse states that God has promised believing men and women gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever, along with good dwellings in the Gardens of Eden, and that God's pleasure is greater than all of this; this is the great triumph. The commentators agree on the eternal nature of this abode and on the superiority of divine pleasure over every delight, as the authentic hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports. They differ, however, on the meaning of 'Adn'. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Tabari take it to mean lasting residence and permanence; Ibn Mas'ud takes it to mean the centre or heart of Paradise; al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and 'Ata' take it to be a palace or a city. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi hold that 'Adn' is a proper name for a specific place in Paradise, citing the verse 'gardens of Eden which the Most Merciful promised'. Several exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, transmit reports describing these dwellings as built of pearls, rubies and chrysolite, though Ibn 'Atiyya finds it inconsistent to assign some features to some gardens when the promise is addressed to all believers. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi argue that divine pleasure exceeds material bounty because it is the source of all happiness. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes between worship out of desire for Paradise or fear of Hell and worship out of love, and discusses both at length. The verse's wording, with 'ridwan' indefinite and placed as subject, is noted by several commentators as emphasising its greatness.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, to be stern with them, and states that their refuge is Hell. The commentators agree that striving against the disbelievers means fighting with the sword. On how to strive against the hypocrites they differ. Ibn Mas'ud, as reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, says it is first with the hand, then the tongue, then the heart, and if one cannot, one should show a stern face. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak take it to mean struggle by speech and harsh words. Al-Hasan and Qatada understand it as enforcing the legal punishments on those who commit their causes. Ibn Kathir reconciles these views by saying they may apply according to circumstances, while al-Tabari prefers that it resembles striving against the disbelievers. Al-ghilza means harshness and roughness, and 'Ata' says the verse abrogated every form of pardon and forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the hypocrite, so long as he professes Islam, is not treated as an openly declared enemy, and al-Tabari explains that the Prophet knew them but left them alone. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim state that striving against the hypocrites is harder and is mainly done through argument. The commentaries also recount the case of al-Jullas ibn Suwayd, who spoke a word of disbelief and then swore he had not said it, and the plot of some hypocrites to harm the Prophet on the road back from Tabuk. Al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Ashur add that the Prophet refrained from killing the hypocrites so that people would not think he killed his own companions.

The verse says the hypocrites swear by God that they said nothing, yet it states that they uttered a word of disbelief, renounced Islam after professing it, and plotted something they did not achieve. The commentators link the passage to the expedition to Tabuk and to remarks made during it. They differ on who spoke: Urwa, Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq name al-Jullas ibn Suwayd, who reportedly said that if what Muhammad says is true, they were worse than donkeys; Qatada names Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who reportedly said that if they returned to Medina the mighty would expel the weak; al-Hasan takes it to be the words of several hypocrites together. As for the unrealised plot, Mujahid relates it to a plan to kill the man who had exposed them, while others describe a scheme to push the Prophet off the steep path at the ridge, foiled by Hudhayfa and Ammar, as recounted by Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi. The phrase saying they found nothing to resent except that God and His Messenger had enriched them is read by most as an ironic statement that praises through the form of blame: what they resent is in fact a favour, the wealth coming from spoils or from a blood-money payment. The commentators agree that the door of repentance remains open, and most reports say al-Jullas repented. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa accept the repentance of a concealed unbeliever, while Malik rejects it unless it comes before he is discovered. The verse ends with a warning of painful punishment in this world and the next for those who persist, with no protector or helper.

This verse describes a group of hypocrites who swore to God that if He granted them wealth from His bounty, they would give charity and be among the righteous. The commentators explain that this means doing what righteous people do with their money, such as maintaining family ties and spending for good causes. When God gave them of His bounty, they grew stingy, broke their word and turned away. As a result, God caused hypocrisy to take root in their hearts until the day they meet Him, because of their broken promise and their lies.

The most widely reported occasion of revelation concerns Tha'laba ibn Hatib al-Ansari, who asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray that he become wealthy. When his flocks multiplied, he withdrew from congregational prayer and Friday prayer, then refused to pay zakat to the collectors. After the Prophet's death he offered his charity to Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman, and each refused it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir regard this narration as having a weak chain, and al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi doubt that it refers to Tha'laba the Badr veteran. Other reports, cited by al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi and al-Jaza'iri, name Mu'tab ibn Qushayr, Jadd ibn Qays, Nabtal ibn al-Harith or Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a.

Commentators differ on what "He caused it to follow them" refers to. Al-Hasan and Qatada take the pronoun to mean their stinginess, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take God as its subject. Al-Hasan al-Basri, quoted by al-Qurtubi, distinguishes hypocrisy of speech, which belonged to the Prophet's time, from hypocrisy of conduct, which continues. Some hold that the vow was only inward, but most say it was spoken aloud. Al-Qurtubi notes that a believer should avoid making promises he does not keep.

This verse in Surah At-Tawba describes a group of hypocrites who had vowed to Allah that, if He gave them wealth, they would give charity and become righteous. When Allah granted them His bounty, they became stingy, turned away from their pledge, and remained averse. The commentators explain that Allah caused hypocrisy to take root in their hearts until the day they meet Him, as a consequence of breaking their promise and lying.

Most exegetes link the verse to Tha'laba ibn Hatib, an Ansari who asked the Prophet to grant him wealth, then refused to pay zakat and died during the caliphate of Uthman. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir narrate this story with its chain, while Ibn Hazm and Ibn Atiyya judge it weak or unacceptable. Al-Mawardi mentions two occasions of revelation, and others, such as Abu Hayyan, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur, name different people, including Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi.

The scholars differ on the kind of hypocrisy meant: some take it as hypocrisy of disbelief, others as hypocrisy of disobedience, as Ibn Atiyya notes. They also disagree about the referent of the pronoun in 'fa-a'qabahum': Zamakhshari and al-Hasan al-Basri relate it to stinginess or to Allah, while al-Razi prefers Allah. Al-Hasan al-Basri held that the three signs in the hadith characterise the hypocrite, whereas others restrict them to the Prophet's time. Al-Qurtubi also reports the debate over whether a vow made only in the heart binds: Malik held that it does, while al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said it does not until spoken.

This verse describes some hypocrites who had pledged to God that, if He gave them wealth from His bounty, they would give charity and be among the righteous. When He did, they became miserly and turned away, so God caused hypocrisy to take root in their hearts until the day they meet Him, as a consequence of breaking their promise and of their lying. The commentators broadly agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Wahidi relate the best-known account, that the verse concerns Tha'laba ibn Hatib al-Ansari, who, once wealthy, refused to pay zakat, and whose gifts were refused by the Prophet and then by Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Hazm nonetheless acknowledge the weakness of this report, and Ibn Hazm judges it false, since Tha'laba was counted among the Badr fighters. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya record other views, naming Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, Jadd ibn Qays and Nabtal ibn al-Harith, and al-Kalbi names Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a. On the pronoun in 'He caused them to follow', al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi attribute the act to God, whereas al-Hasan and Qatada take it as referring to the stinginess. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also discuss whether an unspoken vow binds, a point on which the schools differ, and whether 'meeting' God means death or vision.

In this verse God reminds the hypocrites that He knows their secret, meaning what they conceal in their hearts, such as disbelief or the intention to break their word, and their private conversations, meaning what they say to one another in secret, and that He is the Knower of the unseen, from whom nothing is hidden. The commentators read the verse as a rebuke and a reproach, and as a warning that this knowledge will lead to requital. Al-Tabari explains that the secret conversations were their slander of Islam and its believers, and that the unseen is what hearts conceal and the senses cannot perceive. Al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report that the preceding verses were revealed about Tha'laba ibn Hatib, who vowed to God to give charity and then withheld it, Ibn Kathir noting that most exegetes say so. Al-Dahhak holds that several hypocrites were meant. Al-Razi treats the report that Tha'laba died a hypocrite as a sign of prophethood, while al-Qurtubi finds it more likely that the verse was revealed about others. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan define the secret as hidden hypocrisy and the resolve to break a promise, and the private talk as their disparagement, including calling zakat a poll tax, and they regard these definitions as closely related. Some readers use the second person, addressing the believers.

This passage describes hypocrites who mocked believers who gave voluntarily to charity and ridiculed those who could give only what little they had. According to the commentators, the wealthy donors meant are chiefly Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Asim ibn Adi, and the poor giver is Abu Aqil, who brought a single sa' of dates. The hypocrites accused the generous of showing off and dismissed the modest gift as unnecessary. The phrase "Allah mocks them" is understood by most as Allah requiting them for their mockery, with some seeing a rhetorical symmetry in the wording and others a naming of the punishment after the sin.

The commentators agree that the verse concerns the hypocrites and a charity drive, probably during the expedition to Tabuk, and that mocking and slandering donors is blameworthy. They differ on who exactly is meant. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada name the companions mentioned above, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record other reports, including one naming Abu Khaythama, and Ibn al-Jawzi notes disagreement over Abu Aqil's name. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi take "those who give much" as the sense of the first group, with the second group joined to them in a broader sense.

On language, al-Tabari, al-Farra and al-Zamakhshari distinguish "judh" with a damma, meaning capacity, from "jahd" with a fatha, meaning hardship, while others treat the two forms as synonyms and al-Shabi is cited as drawing the same distinction. Al-Razi adds that the small gift of a poor man may weigh more with God than the large gift of a rich one.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that asking forgiveness for the hypocrites or not doing so is the same: God will not forgive them even if he asks forgiveness seventy times, because they disbelieved in God and His Messenger, and because wickedness has become a settled trait in them that denies them guidance. The commentators agree that seventy stands for a great number rather than a fixed limit, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur explain, since the Arabs use seven and seventy for abundance. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and others report that the Prophet ﷺ said he would exceed seventy after the revelation, but al-Zamakhshari notes that the judge 'Iyad did not accept this report as authentic, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir favour the reading of an option given to the Prophet that was then settled by the verse in Surat al-Munafiqun. Al-Razi argues that the Prophet could not have asked forgiveness for an unbeliever, whereas al-Alusi replies that praying for the living is permitted as a means of seeking forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the Prophet showed great mercy, and several commentators say the request may have served to win over some hypocrites. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya also discuss the denial of guidance, which Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi take to mean that God does not grant the guidance that leads to the goal because of their wickedness.

This verse describes the hypocrites who stayed behind during the expedition of Tabuk. They rejoiced at remaining in Medina in defiance of the Messenger of God, disliked sacrificing their wealth and lives in God's cause, and told one another not to march in the heat. God instructs His Prophet to answer that the fire of Hell is far hotter, if only they understood. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, agree that the verse concerns the hypocrites of Tabuk, that the heat was severe at the time, and that the reply is a rebuke: whoever flees a brief heat only to fall into eternal punishment shows extreme ignorance, as al-Zamakhshari puts it. The word khilaf may mean 'after' the Messenger's departure, following Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash, or 'opposition' to him, following al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj, and both readings are supported by variant recitations. On the phrase 'let them laugh little and weep much', Ibn Abbas and Qatada read it as a contrast between the short life of this world and endless weeping in the next, while others take it as a statement in the form of a command. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that rejoicing at staying behind and disliking jihad clearly reveal hypocrisy, without settling the precise sense of yafqahun.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses the hypocrites and those who stayed behind during the expedition of Tabuk. They rejoiced at remaining in Medina after the Prophet set out, refused to fight with their wealth and lives, and said to one another: do not march in this heat. The imperative form announces what will happen: their laughter in this world will be brief, since the world is perishing, and their weeping in the Hereafter will be abundant, since it will be endless. Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Rabi ibn Khuthaym and Ibn Zayd hold that the little laughter refers to the span of life and the much weeping to eternal punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite reports that the people of the Fire will weep until tears turn to blood. Al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani say the imperative carries the sense of a future statement, and that the little laughter may mean none at all. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress that the imperative form marks an inevitable decree. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi read laughter and weeping as figurative expressions of joy and grief. Ibn 'Ashur follows the same reading and adds that the laughter reflects the hypocrites' satisfaction at having deceived the Prophet. Ibn Sa'di emphasises the pride they take in their disobedience. Across these views, the final punishment corresponds to their deeds, namely their hypocrisy and their sins.

This verse says that if God brings the Prophet back from the Tabuk expedition to a group of those who stayed behind and who ask his permission to go out with him again, he should tell them that they will never go out with him or fight an enemy alongside him, because they were content to sit back the first time; so they should remain with those who stayed behind. Most commentators understand the group to be hypocrites, and note that the word 'a group' is used because some of them repented or had a valid excuse; Qatada reports that there were twelve men. On the meaning of 'al-khalifin', Ibn Abbas takes it to mean men who stayed behind without excuse, while al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean women, children and the weak. Al-Tabari judges that the masculine form covers the mixed group and rejects Qatada's reading, since the plural for women alone would not take that form. Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari also accept the masculine as inclusive, while Ibn Atiyya finds the reading 'corrupt' forced. On 'the first time', al-Mawardi offers either the first time they were called or the time before they asked permission, but most take it to be Tabuk. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain the refusal as a punishment that exposes their hypocrisy, and al-Sha'rawi adds that their names were removed from the list of fighters. Several scholars link the verse to the ruling that the Prophet should not pray over the hypocrites after their deaths.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ not to pray over any of the hypocrites who die and not to stand at their graves to pray for them or to attend their burial, because they disbelieved in God and His Messenger and died in that state. The commentators report that the verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, over whom the Prophet ﷺ had prayed after giving him his shirt, and that the prohibition came afterward. They agree that the ruling applies to anyone whose hypocrisy is known, and that the prohibition rests on the disbelief in which the person died. The accounts differ on what happened: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Jabir and Qatada, and most of the transmissions, say the Prophet did pray over him, while al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan cite reports that Gabriel stopped him before he prayed; Ibn Hajar and Ibn Kathir regard some of these reports as weak. Abu Hayyan sees the prohibition as a second punishment and a lasting disgrace, and al-Razi as a means of humiliating them. Al-Zamakhshari explains the gift of the shirt as a reward for the kindness shown to al-Abbas when he was captured at Badr, and al-Qurtubi considers this the sounder view. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report that the Prophet said his shirt would not benefit the man, but that he hoped a thousand of his people would become Muslims because of it. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir understand the prayer as supplication and seeking forgiveness, and Ibn Kathir notes that standing at the grave includes pausing to supplicate. Ibn Sa'di draws from the verse the permissibility of praying over believers and visiting their graves to pray for them.

This verse tells the Prophet, and through him the believers, not to be impressed by the wealth and children of the hypocrites, because God intends only to punish them through these things in this world, through the worries, burdens and calamities they bring, until their souls depart while they are disbelievers. The commentators agree on the core message: a warning against admiring the riches of those who show faith without possessing it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Suddi's report cited by al-Tabari stress that these possessions become a regret at death and a burden in the hereafter. Al-Mawardi gives three possible meanings of the punishment: the anxiety of guarding these possessions, the misfortunes that strike them, or punishment in the hereafter for the way they were earned and spent, and Ibn al-Anbari adds a fourth by reversing the order of the words. On the question of repetition, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan see it as emphasis on an important matter that must not be forgotten, while al-Farisi holds that the two verses concern different groups and so there is no repetition. Al-Razi and al-Biqa'i explain the differences in wording between the two verses, notably the omission of "life" before "this world", to signify the lowliness of the worldly life. Ibn 'Ashur notes that this verse describes the state of these possessions after death. Sayyid Qutb and Ibn Sa'di emphasise that these people's wealth is a humiliation rather than an honour, and that the believer should not respect it.

This verse describes the hypocrites' reaction when a surah is revealed commanding belief in God and jihad alongside His Messenger: those among them with wealth ask permission to stay behind and say, leave us to be with those who sit out. The commentators agree that tawl means wealth and ability, and that asking for exemption while being able to go shows indolence. On the word khawalif, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid take it to mean women, while Ibn Qutayba and those who follow him read it as the lowliest and most worthless of people; al-Farra and Ibn al-Anbari also offer other readings, including women left behind in their homes. Opinions also differ on which surah is meant: most hold that it is any surah containing the command to believe and fight, whereas Muqatil, al-Zamakhshari and others identify it as Surat al-Tawba. Al-Wahidi and al-Razi note that the command to believe, addressed to hypocrites, means believing in the heart as the tongue professes, and al-Razi adds that it may also mean persisting in faith. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Kathir and others report that the verse concerns Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays and Mu'attib ibn Qushayr.
