On the phrase that their hearts were sealed, Ibn Kathir explains it as the result of their refusal to fight, al-Razi as a powerful motive toward disbelief, and al-Hasan as a leaning toward disbelief so strong that faith seems dead within them. The common thread is that they fail to grasp the success that striving brings and the loss that staying behind entails.

The commentators explain that this verse describes hypocrites who, when a surah was revealed commanding them to believe in God and to fight alongside His Messenger, asked the Prophet for exemption, namely the wealthy among them. They were content to remain with the "khawalif". Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, al-Farra, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, identify these as the women who stayed behind in the homes, so the verse rebukes the hypocrites for placing themselves on the level of women. Ibn Qutayba, al-Nahhas and the authors of al-Jalalayn also mention the sense of base or worthless people, which is close to the first meaning.

On the phrase "their hearts were sealed, so they do not understand", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as God sealing their hearts because of their refusal to go out to fight, which leaves them unable to grasp the success that jihad brings and the harm of staying behind. Al-Razi explains the seal as a strong motive towards disbelief, a view linked to al-Hasan's description of a heart so inclined to unbelief that it is as though dead to faith. The Mu'tazilites regard it as a mark in the heart. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as an image of the heart's refusal to accept guidance.

The commentators also connect the verse to what follows. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan note that the Messenger and the believers struggled with their wealth and their lives, and that good things and success belong to them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy read these good things as benefits of both worlds, while others take them to be the houris or the spoils of war.

This verse contrasts the hypocrites who stayed behind from fighting with the Prophet and the believers who joined him, striving with their wealth and their lives. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that if these people hold back, someone better and more sincere has already risen to the struggle. The "good things" (al-khayrat) promised to them are read by al-Tabari as the rewards of the Hereafter, while Ibn Kathir places them in the high gardens of Paradise. Ibn 'Ashur, al-Zamakhshari and al-Shawkani extend the word to the benefits of both worlds, such as victory and spoils in this life and Paradise in the next. Al-Mawardi lists four possible meanings: the spoils and benefits of jihad, generous gifts, the reward of the Hereafter, and the maidens of Paradise. Al-Sam'ani reports from Ibn 'Abbas that its exact meaning is known only to God. Several scholars, including al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi, favour the sense of the maidens, citing the verse about good and beautiful women in Surat al-Rahman. The word is the plural of khayra, a feminine form of "good", illustrated by a classical line quoted by al-Tabari and Abu 'Ubayda. As for success (al-falah), al-Tabari understands it as remaining forever in the gardens, al-Razi as being spared punishment, and al-Baydawi as reaching what one seeks. The commentators agree that the passage presents the conduct of the hypocrites and of the sincere believers as opposites.

This verse states that God has prepared for the Prophet and for those who believed with him gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever without dying or leaving, and that this is the great triumph. Most commentators take it as spelling out the otherworldly reward that the previous verse mentioned in general terms as "the good things". Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn Sa'di hold that these good things cover both the benefits of this world and of the next, while the gardens refer to the bliss of the afterlife. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi understand the word khayrat to cover everything excellent, such as victory, spoils and honour. Al-Mawardi lists four possible meanings: the gains of struggle, generous gifts, future reward, and the maidens of paradise. Al-Hasan, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Shawkani report that the term refers to beautiful women of paradise, citing the verse about good and beautiful women there. Al-Tabari also reports that Ibn 'Abbas held its meaning to be known only to God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the particle "but" contrasts the hypocrites who stayed behind with the believers who fought, and that if the former hold back, someone better has taken up the struggle. Al-Razi reads the great triumph as an exalted rank, al-Sha'rawi as a lasting grace, and al-Nasafi observes that the verb "prepared" shows the garden already exists.

This verse tells of Bedouins from the areas around Madinah who came to the Prophet ﷺ asking permission to stay behind, while others remained without offering any excuse, having lied to Allah and His Messenger in claiming faith; Allah warns them of a painful punishment. The commentators agree that those who stayed without excuse were hypocrites. They differ over those who came with excuses. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, followed by Ibn Kathir who considers this the more apparent view, held that these men were sincere in their excuse, and some name men from the tribe of Ghifar. Qatada and al-Hasan held that they were lying and that Allah did not accept their excuse. The disagreement extends to the recitation: the form with a shadda, al-mu'adhdhirun, may mean 'those who make excuses' according to al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari, or 'those who feign an excuse' according to al-Jawhari and al-Zamakhshari. The unshadda form, al-mu'dhirun, means 'those who have a valid excuse', a reading attributed to Ibn 'Abbas. The commentators report several occasions of revelation: the clan of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan, or the men of Ghifar. The punishment is understood as death or captivity in this world and the Fire in the next. Some note that the word 'min' indicates only part of them, since some would later believe.

This verse states that no blame falls on those who stay behind for a genuine excuse: the weak, such as the elderly, children and the frail, the sick, such as the blind and the chronically ill, and the poor who lack the means to equip themselves for the expedition. The exemption holds on condition that they are sincere toward God and His Messenger, meaning they have upright intentions and do what they can, encouraging the struggle and watching over the homes of those who fight. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the 'doers of good' to be precisely these sincere excused people, who are neither blamed nor punished, and God is forgiving and merciful toward them. The commentators agree on this core ruling. They differ on who the 'weak' are: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada identify them as the disabled and the elderly, others as children, women or the insane, while Ibn al-Jawzi holds that the correct meaning covers those weakened by chronic affliction, blindness, old age or frailty of body. Al-Qurtubi defines sincere counsel as purity of intention free from deceit, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it to mean faith and obedience in both public and private. Al-Razi draws from the verse the principle that the presumption of innocence and freedom from obligation stands unless proven otherwise. The next verse describes those who came to the Prophet asking to be given mounts for the campaign and turned away weeping for lack of them. The reports differ on their identity, naming the Banu Muqarrin, Ibn Mughaffal, or Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his companions, or seven men called the weepers. They also differ on what they asked for: mounts according to Ibn 'Abbas, provisions according to Anas, and sandals according to al-Hasan.

This verse describes men who came to the Prophet ﷺ asking him to provide them with mounts for the campaign. He had nothing to give them, so they turned away weeping, grieved that they could not spend for the cause. The commentators differ on who they were. Al-Tabari reports, through Mujahid, that they were the sons of Muqarrin of the tribe of Muzayna, while other views name 'Irbad ibn Sariya, 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal or 'A'idh ibn 'Amr. Ibn Ishaq and Muhammad ibn Ka'b speak of seven men from various tribes, known as the weepers, and Ibn Kathir lists several names. As to what they asked for, Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes say a mount, Anas ibn Malik says provisions, and al-Hasan says sandals; the view that they wanted mounts is the most common. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, note that their grief shows the sincerity of their wish to fight. Ibn Kathir cites a report that those kept back by a genuine excuse share the reward of the fighters. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud draw attention to the eloquence of the phrase 'their eyes overflow with tears', as the eye is described as if it were entirely tears pouring forth.

This verse states that blame and punishment fall only on the wealthy who were able to go out for jihad but asked the Prophet for permission to stay behind without a valid excuse. They chose to remain with the khawalif, which the commentators explain as women and children left at home. Al-Tabari says these men acted out of hypocrisy and doubt about God's promise, while al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi give the same plain sense. Ibn Kathir focuses on the difference between genuine excuses and pretexts, and notes that the earlier verses excuse the truly weak. Al-Razi reads the phrase about God sealing their hearts as meaning that they were left in neglect, so they could not see the worldly and religious benefits of jihad. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan discuss whether the word innama restricts the meaning, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that the restriction is relative, referring back to the people excused in the verses before. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the clause about their willingness is a resumptive clause giving the cause of the request. Al-Sha'rawi understands wealth to include physical strength and health, not only money. Most commentators link the verse to the hypocrites who stayed behind during the expedition to Tabuk, and Ibn Kathir reports several differing names for them without preferring one.

This verse concerns the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk without a valid excuse, and who offer excuses to the believers upon their return. God instructs His Messenger to tell them not to make excuses, for they will not be believed, since God has informed him of their reports and of what their hearts conceal. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that the prohibition rests on the fact that one who apologizes seeks to be believed, and when he knows he will be denounced as a liar, he refrains. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan add that the very revelation of their secrets is the reason for withholding belief. The phrase 'God will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger' is read by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as meaning that God will observe whether they repent from hypocrisy or persist in it, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi take it as both a warning and an opening for repentance, and al-Sha'rawi stresses that the door of return is left open. The commentators agree that the return to the One who knows the unseen and the seen refers to resurrection, and that the recompense will concern what was done in secret and in public. Al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi report, following Ibn 'Abbas, that these hypocrites numbered about eighty men, among them Abdullah ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays and Mu'attib ibn Qushayr. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the address is directed to the Muslims, since the hypocrites offered their excuses both to the Prophet and to the believers, and that the negation carries the sense of discouraging them from expecting acceptance.

In this verse God announces that the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk will swear oaths to the believers when they return to Medina, hoping to be left alone and not reproached. The commentators explain the command to turn away from them in two closely related ways. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as abandoning rebuke and blame, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud understand it as giving up on reforming them, since they are impurities that reproach cannot cleanse. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan stress that it means avoidance and disdain rather than pardon. All agree that "rijs" denotes an inner, moral filth and that their final abode is Hell as recompense for what they earned. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the verse was revealed about hypocrites who stayed behind, and that the Prophet ordered that they not be sat with or spoken to; Muqatil links its revelation to Abdullah ibn Ubayy. Al-Razi notes that the verse forbids being pleased with them, since God is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the ruling to extend to anyone known for a blameworthy innovation, whereas others confine it to those hypocrites.

This verse reports that the hypocrites swear to the believers seeking their approval after staying behind from the expedition to Tabuk. If the believers approve of them, it will not benefit them, for God does not approve of the defiantly disobedient people. The commentators broadly agree that these were hypocrites who stayed behind without excuse, and that their oaths were false, aimed at winning favour rather than expressing repentance. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain that their purpose in swearing was to gain benefit in this world, and that the believers' approval alone is useless against God's displeasure. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi read the verse as a prohibition on the believers approving of them, noting that the approval of the faithful does not entail God's approval. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as an indirect warning against reconciling with the hypocrites. Most scholars, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, take the word fasiqin to mean those who go beyond obedience. Accounts of who was meant vary: Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil name Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr and especially 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. Abu Hayyan notes that the omission of the sworn oath echoes the earlier mention, and that the conditional form is used because approval is an inward matter.

This verse states that the Bedouins are more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy than the people of the towns, and are more likely to be ignorant of the limits of what God sent down to His Messenger. The commentators agree on the causes: distance from gatherings of knowledge and from hearing the Quran and learning the Sunna, together with harshness of manner and hardness of heart. Qatada explained that the limits are the prophetic traditions. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report the account of Zayd ibn Sawhan, who quoted the verse when a Bedouin did not know which hand is cut for theft. They differ on the meaning of the limits. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi take them as the obligatory duties and the laws; al-Razi includes the degrees of evidence for God's oneness, prophethood and the afterlife, along with the rulings; al-Mawardi adds the warning against opposing the Prophet and shirking jihad. Al-Qurtubi draws several rulings: Bedouins have no share of the spoils unless they fight, and the scholars differ on accepting their testimony and on their leading prayer, Abu Hanifa accepting it while al-Shafi'i requires uprightness. Ibn 'Ashur reads the superlatives as expressing strength of disbelief rather than an exact comparison. Most exegetes take the comparison to be with the hypocrites of Medina, while al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di note that the verse describes the general trend and not every individual.

This verse describes a group of Bedouin Arabs who regard what they spend in Allah's cause as a forced loss, expecting no reward from it and no protection from punishment, since they spend out of show or fear of the Muslims. They wait for misfortunes to befall the believers, and God calls down evil on them: the bad turn comes back upon them, not upon the believers. The commentators agree that these are hypocrites among the Bedouins. Al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd report that they see their spending as a burden, out of fear of being raided or fought. Al-Mawardi explains that maghram means taking on what is not obligatory, and that dawa'ir means a blessing turning into its opposite. According to al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya, this waiting may take the form of openly declaring disbelief or seizing a chance for revenge; others took it to mean waiting for the death of the Prophet and the victory of the polytheists.

Readers differ on the vowel of the word al-sau'. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the sin, while the others read it with a fatha. Al-Farra' and al-Tabari prefer the fatha, which is a verbal noun meaning the badness of the circle, whereas the damma means harm, punishment or calamity. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the two readings are close in meaning.

The next verse separates out those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, who take their spending as a means of drawing near to Allah and of obtaining the Prophet's prayers. The commentators identify them as the sons of Muqarrin of Muzayna, and God will admit them into His mercy.

This verse describes the believing Bedouins, who believe in God and the Last Day and who treat what they spend in God's cause, whether in fighting or in charity, as a means of drawing near to God, together with seeking the Prophet's supplication for them. Most commentators understand the prayers (salawat) as the Prophet's supplications and pleas for forgiveness, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Biqa'i take them as simple invocation. Mujahid and al-Tabari report that the verse concerns the sons of Muqarrin of the tribe of Muzayna, while Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir extend it to Aslam, Ghifar and Juhayna, and al-Kalbi is cited to the same effect. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur read the phrase 'Surely it is a means of nearness for them' as a divine testimony to the giver's sincere intention, and the particle 'sa' in 'He will admit them' as affirming a certain promise. As for the pronoun 'it', most scholars refer it to the expenditures, while others refer it to the Prophet's prayers. Warsh reads 'qurubatun' with a damma, while the rest read it with a sukun. The commentators conclude that God is Forgiving and Merciful, and that He will admit these believers into His mercy, which Ibn Kathir and others understand as Paradise.

This verse states that the foremost emigrants and helpers, and those who followed them in excellence, earned Allah's pleasure and were pleased with Him, and that He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they abide forever; this is the great triumph. The commentators differ on who the foremost (al-sabiqun al-awwalun) were. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Sirin and Qatada take them to be those who prayed toward both qiblas; ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah says the people of Badr; al-Sha'bi says those present at the Pledge of Ridwan at Hudaybiyya. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Nakha'i held Abu Bakr to be the first man to embrace Islam after Khadija, while others named ʿAli, and al-Zuhri named Zayd ibn Haritha. Ibn Ishaq noted that each was foremost in a different respect. Al-Razi preferred that the reference is to those who were first in emigration and in helping the Prophet, a view few others adopted. ʿUmar read « wal-anṣāru » in the nominative; Ubayy ibn Kaʿb corrected him about the waw before « alladhina ittabaʿuhum », and ʿUmar deferred to him. Most hold that those who follow with excellence are the later generations who walked in their path until the Last Day; Ibn Zayd extends this to all believers until the Hour, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi require that the following be good in deeds and words. The passage then turns to the hypocrites among the Bedouins and the people of Madina, whom the Prophet does not know and whom God will punish twice before a great torment, and to those who confessed their sins, such as Abu Lubaba and his companions, for whom God may relent, as well as those whose fate is left to God's decision.

God tells His Prophet that among the Bedouins around Medina there are hypocrites, and that among the people of Medina too there are men who persisted in hypocrisy and trained themselves in it until they became masters of it. The Prophet cannot recognise them, but God alone knows their true state. The commentators explain that the verb marradu means they clung to it obstinately and did not repent, and some add that they became insolent in it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the Prophet's lack of knowledge concerns their identities, not whether hypocrites existed among his companions, and Ibn Kathir cites the report of Jubayr ibn Mut'im in support. On the phrase 'We shall punish them twice', the opinions differ widely. Ibn 'Abbas, in the best-known report, says the first punishment was their public exposure when the Prophet had them expelled from the mosque, and the second was the punishment of the grave. Mujahid mentions killing and captivity, or hunger; Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to be worldly trials affecting their wealth and children; al-Hasan refers to the zakat taken from their property; Ibn Ishaq to their resentment at Islam's growth. Al-Tabari concludes that one of the two is the punishment of the grave, without deciding the other. The great punishment they are returned to is, for nearly all the commentators, the Fire of Hell. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi gather these views, and al-Razi offers several readings tied to the three stages of life.

This verse concerns a group of believers, not hypocrites, who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk without valid excuse, then admitted their wrong and repented. Most commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, hold that it was revealed about them, with Abu Lubaba among them. They had tied themselves to the mosque pillars until the Prophet released them after the revelation. The reported number varies between three, five, six, seven, eight and ten. Al-Tabari concludes that it refers to a group who lagged behind at Tabuk. Mujahid links it only to Abu Lubaba and the Banu Qurayza episode, while al-Zuhri links it to his absence from Tabuk. Ibn Abbas and Abu Uthman al-Nahdi take it as general for any sinner who mixes good and bad deeds, and Abu Uthman called it the most hopeful verse in the Quran. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that confessing sin alone is not repentance, and that the divine word 'perhaps' is taken by many as a firm promise. Commentators differ on the 'good deed' and 'bad deed': some say the good was past jihad and the bad the present absence, others that the good was confession and repentance and the bad the offence itself. The following verse orders the Prophet to take a charity from their wealth, and scholars differ on whether it was obligatory zakat or a special expiation for these men.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to take from the wealth of those who admitted their sins and mixed good deeds with bad an alms that purifies them and causes them to grow, to bless them and to pray for them, for his prayer brings tranquillity to their hearts and assurance that their repentance is accepted. The commentators agree that the verse concerns those who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk, above all Abu Lubaba and his companions who tied themselves to the mosque pillars, and that the Prophet took a third of their wealth, as reported by Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Tabari and Mujahid. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the alms as an expiation for sin, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan note that the pronoun may refer to property owners in general. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that purification is intensified by cleansing and that growth means increased blessing in wealth. The scholars differ on the kind of alms: Ibn Abbas and Ikrima take it to be the obligatory zakat, Ibn Zayd and the majority take it to be voluntary charity, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi see here a basis for the obligation of zakat. As for sakan, Ibn Abbas reads it as mercy, Qatada as dignity, al-Kalbi as reassurance and Abu Ubayda as steadiness. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir also note the recommendation that the collector pray for the giver, and al-Shafi'i specifies the words to be said.

This verse states that God alone accepts the repentance of His servants and receives their charity, and that He is the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful. Al-Tabari explains that it assures believers that accepting the repentance of the hypocrites and receiving their alms is not in the hands of the Prophet but of God alone. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the pronoun huwa adds emphasis and exclusivity, meaning no prophet or angel can do this. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi take the verb 'to take' to mean 'to accept', and Ibn 'Atiyya also notes that it may mean ordaining charity. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan observe that 'an' conveys pardon and overlooking of sins. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir, cite the hadith of Abu Hurayra that charity falls into God's hand before it reaches the beggar and that He makes it grow. Al-Qurtubi reads this as a figurative expression of acceptance and reward, without describing God's form. Most scholars take the question as a rhetorical affirmation intended to encourage repentance and charity. Some readings change the addressees: the verb may refer to the repentant, or to the hypocrites who had not repented, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that the verse is a general encouragement to those who had delayed. The common meaning is that repentance and charity are accepted by God, who forgives and shows mercy to those who turn back to Him.

This verse tells the Prophet to say to those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk and confessed their sins: act as you wish, for God, His Messenger and the believers will see your deeds, and then you will be returned to the One who knows the unseen and the seen, who will inform you of what you did and repay you for it. The commentators agree that the verse carries a warning and a threat. They differ, however, on who is addressed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it mainly as addressed to the repentant or the excused, while Ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that it concerns those who made excuses without repenting. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi say it may cover both groups, its aim being to encourage the unrepentant to repent.

Scholars also differ on what the seeing by the Prophet and the believers means. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi explain it as the Prophet being informed by God, and the believers perceiving it through the love God places in their hearts for the righteous and the hatred for corruptors. Al-Razi understands it as the news of the deed spreading among people, citing a hadith about a deed done in a sealed rock. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the believers' seeing may be their testimony after death. Al-Razi, who draws from this verse the claim that God sees perceptible things, rejects the reading of seeing as mere knowledge.

Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the verse combines encouragement and warning, while Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi point out the future tense with the particle sin, which stresses the certainty of the recompense.

This verse describes a third group among those who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk: people whose matter is held in suspense, neither punished nor forgiven yet, until God decides. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, identify them as Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya and Murara ibn al-Rabi', reported through Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Dahhak and Qatada. They were not hypocrites: unlike Abu Lubaba and his companions, they did not come to the Prophet to offer excuses, so he ordered the Muslims to shun them, and this lasted fifty nights until their repentance was revealed. Al-Razi notes that the difference from the previous group is that these did not hasten to repent. Al-Hasan and al-Asamm, by contrast, take the verse to refer to hypocrites. Commentators debate the word "imma": al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain it as expressing the believers' uncertainty or as a division of possibilities, and al-Razi answers the objection of al-Jubba'i, who argued from it that God forgives only the repentant. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di conclude that God knows their state and is wise in what He does with them.

This verse describes a group of hypocrites who built a mosque with a harmful purpose. According to the commentators, it was a place of worship built to harm the mosque of Quba', to disbelieve in God and His Messenger, to divide the believers between two mosques, and to prepare for and await the arrival of Abu 'Amir the monk, who had fought the Prophet earlier before fleeing to Syria. The exegetes agree that they were about twelve men, though they differ on the names. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu al-Su'ud report that the Prophet, on returning from Tabuk, ordered the mosque demolished and burned, and the site was turned into a rubbish heap. Al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq relate that the builders swore they had intended only good, meaning comfort for the sick and those out in the rain, but God proved them liars. On God's words 'Never stand therein,' all understand a prohibition on praying there. By contrast, the commentators identify the mosque 'founded on piety from the first day' in two ways: Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Urwa and Qatada say it is Quba' mosque, while Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri say it is the Prophet's mosque in Medina, a view al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer, and Ibn 'Ashur tries to reconcile the two. Most note that 'men who love to purify themselves' praises the people of Quba' for cleansing with water after relieving themselves, though some read it as purification from sin through repentance. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Arabi draw the rule that any mosque built to harm or for show must be pulled down, and that a second mosque may not be built beside one that suffices for the neighbourhood. All conclude that the verse exposes the falsehood of the hypocrites' oaths.

This verse concerns the mosque of harm, built by hypocrites to injure the believers and split their community, and it forbids the Prophet ﷺ ever to pray in it. It then praises the mosque founded on piety from the first day, and the men who love to purify themselves. The commentators agree that the mosque of harm was built by hypocrites from the Banu Amr ibn Awf and their associates, aiming to cause harm, sow division, and prepare a refuge for Abu Amir the monk, who had fought the Prophet. The Prophet ﷺ ordered it demolished and burned, and it became a rubbish heap. On the mosque founded on piety, opinions differ. Ibn Abbas, Ata, Urwa, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and al-Dahhak identify it as the mosque of Quba, relying on the context and its earlier foundation than the Medina mosque. Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab identify it as the Prophet's mosque in Medina, citing the authentic hadith in which the Prophet said it is this mosque of mine. Some reconcile the views by holding that the description fits both, a position al-Suhayli also takes. On the phrase those who love to purify themselves, most explain it as purification with water after relieving oneself, the people of Quba combining stones and water; al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliya understand it as purification from sins through repentance; al-Kalbi and Qatada speak of washing the anus with water. The report that fever was a purification, mentioned by al-Baghawi, is not accepted by all, and Ibn Kathir judges it weak. Finally, God's love for the purified means, for most, His good pleasure and kindness toward them.

This verse sets two foundations side by side: the man who builds his structure on piety toward God and seeking His pleasure, and the man who builds it on the crumbling edge of a ravine, so that it collapses with its builder into the fire of Hell. The commentators read it as a parable, the rhetorical question needing no answer. All agree that the second structure is the mosque of harm built by the hypocrites. On the first, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak identify it as the mosque of Quba, while Ibn 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri identify it as the Prophet's mosque in Medina, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya favour the reports supporting this second view. As for the collapse, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah report that it happened literally, with smoke rising from the spot, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read it as a figure for the falsehood that drags its builder down. On the phrase about a doubt remaining in their hearts, Ibn 'Abbas explains it as doubt, Habib ibn Abi Thabit as spite, al-Suddi as resentment, and al-Razi as doubt about prophethood or about God's forgiveness. On the phrase 'unless their hearts are cut to pieces', Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean death, while Sufyan takes it to mean repentance.

This verse describes how the structure built by the hypocrites, meant to harm the believers, promote disbelief, divide them and serve as a station for one who had fought God and His Messenger, remains a source of doubt and hypocrisy in their hearts. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak take the word rayb to mean doubt, while al-Suddi, Habib and al-Mubarrad understand it as rancour and rage at the demolition of the building, and al-Kalbi as grief and regret over having built it. As for the phrase 'unless their hearts are broken', Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak say it means until they die, al-Thawri says it means repentance so deep that the heart breaks with remorse, and 'Ikrima says it will happen in their graves. Readers differ between taqatta'a with a fatha and tuqatta'a with a damma; al-Tabari holds that both readings come to much the same meaning, since hearts break only when God breaks them. The commentators agree that the verse describes the lasting effect of this mosque on its builders, and that God knows their intentions and is wise in ordering its demolition. Reports cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi state that the building was torn down and burned on the Prophet's orders.

This verse says that God has bought from the believers their souls and their possessions, meaning that He accepts what they devote to His cause and repays them with Paradise. The language of purchase is a metaphor: the commentators explain that a believer who fights in God's way, whether he is killed or spends his wealth, receives Paradise in return, whether he kills or is killed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi relate that it was revealed at the pledge of al-Aqaba, when the Ansar asked for Paradise in exchange for protecting the Prophet, and cried out that the bargain was profitable and they would neither cancel nor seek cancellation. Al-Hasan and Qatada say that God set a high price for them. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya note that some read it as a general rule for every fighter until the Last Day. Readers differ on the order of 'they kill and are killed': al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take the inversion to stress steadfastness after comrades fall. The verse says this promised Paradise is written in the Torah, the Gospel and the Quran; al-Razi draws from this that every community was commanded to fight with a reward attached. None is more faithful to his promise than God, and the believers are told to rejoice in this transaction, which is the great triumph. Several commentators then list nine qualities of those who make this contract: repentance, worship, praise, sayahah, bowing and prostration, enjoining good, forbidding evil and guarding God's limits. On 'sayahah', Ibn Abbas and most scholars take it to mean fasting, Ata takes it as fighting, and Ikrima as seeking knowledge; none of them settles the matter.

The verse describes the believers whom God has bought, with their selves and wealth, in exchange for Paradise, through nine qualities: they repent from polytheism and sins, worship God sincerely, praise Him in hardship and ease, fast (according to most), bow and prostrate in prayer, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and keep God's limits. The Prophet is commanded to give these believers good news.

The commentators agree that these are the qualities of complete believers, and that bowing and prostrating refer to prayer. They also agree that enjoining good and forbidding evil covers calling to monotheism, obedience to God and His Messenger, and opposing polytheism and innovation. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas say the repentant are those who turned away from polytheism and hypocrisy, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that repentance covers every sin, since the word is general.

Opinions differ on the sa'ihun. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada take them to be fasting people, 'Ata' says they are warriors, 'Ikrima says seekers of knowledge, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd says emigrants. Abu Muslim takes them as travellers engaged in jihad or good works. Ibn Kathir notes that this wandering does not mean withdrawing to mountains or deserts.

A hadith cited by some commentators calls the jihad, or fasting, the wandering of this community. As for the waw in 'wal-nahunna', some regard it as the so-called waw of eight, which others, such as Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur, reject, seeing only a conjunction linking two related qualities.

This verse states that it is not fitting for the Prophet or the believers to ask forgiveness for polytheists, even close relatives, once it has become clear that they died in polytheism and belong to the Blazing Fire. The commentators agree that seeking forgiveness for a polytheist who died in disbelief is forbidden, and that the verse severs loyalty between believers and polytheists even when they are relatives. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take the prohibition to concern the dead, while praying for the guidance of a living person whose conversion is hoped for is permitted, a view also noted by al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan. Al-Sa'di adds that forgiveness for a disbeliever would be of no benefit. Some, following Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, understand istighfar here as the funeral prayer. The case of Abraham praying for his father is explained by all as a promise made to his father; he disavowed him when it became clear that his father was an enemy of God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report this happened at the father's death, whereas Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr place it on the Day of Resurrection, when the father is turned into a hyena. As for the occasion of revelation, the best known version links it to the death of Abu Talib, the Prophet's uncle, while other reports concern his mother Amina and the believers who wished to pray for their parents. Ibn Kathir considers several of these narrations weak, and Ibn 'Ashur holds the surah to be late, which makes a direct link with Abu Talib's death in Mecca doubtful.

This verse explains that Abraham's plea for forgiveness for his polytheist father was only fulfilling a promise he had made to him: he had said he would ask God to forgive him, hoping he would believe. When it became clear that his father was an enemy of God, either through his death in disbelief or through a revelation that he would never believe, Abraham disowned him and stopped praying for him. God then describes him as awwah, meaning one who often laments and humbles himself, and halim, meaning forbearing and patient toward offense. The commentators agree that this passage clarifies Abraham's case and comes before the prohibition on believers asking forgiveness for idolaters who are destined for the Fire.

The meaning of awwah has several explanations. Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayd ibn Umayr take it to mean one who calls on God often, al-Hasan and Qatada to mean merciful toward God's servants, and according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata' and Ikrima it means one who is certain in faith, with Ikrima adding that the word is Abyssinian. Others understand it as one who glorifies God, who recites the Qur'an a great deal, or who sighs in fear of the Fire and of his sins, a sense al-Tabari favours by pointing to the root in the sigh of lament. Ka'b al-Ahbar reported that Abraham often said, 'Oh, the Fire!'

As for forbearance, the commentators understand it as pardoning wrongs and patience under insult, recalling that Abraham endured his father's threat to stone him. Opinions also differ on who made the promise and when Abraham came to understand his father's state.

This verse states that God does not judge a people He has guided to be astray until He has made clear to them what they must guard against. Once a prohibition is explained and someone still persists, they deserve to be led astray. Al-Tabari and Mujahid connect the verse to the question of seeking forgiveness for polytheist relatives: some believers had prayed for their dead associator kin before the prohibition came, and feared for them. The verse reassures them that no one is held accountable for what they did before the rule was clarified. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi widen this to every prohibition, and Ibn Sa'di sees in it proof that the divine law covers everything people need.

On the occasion of revelation, al-Wahidi, al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan report, through Ibn 'Abbas, that some Bedouins embraced Islam and prayed toward Jerusalem and fasted the white days, then on returning found the Prophet praying toward the Ka'ba and fasting Ramadan, and asked whether they were now astray. Al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi also mention other accounts, including that of those who prayed for dead polytheists. Al-Razi notes that the Mu'tazila read "to lead astray" as pronouncing someone misguided, a reading rejected by Abu Bakr al-Anbari and Abu Hayyan. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi use the verse to argue that the heedless person is not accountable for what he cannot know through reason, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that what reason itself grasps, such as truthfulness or returning a trust, needs no revealed text. The verse closes by affirming God's knowledge of everything, and the next verse speaks of His dominion over heaven and earth.

This verse states that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, that He gives life and causes death, and that people have no protector or helper apart from Him. Al-Tabari reads it as an exhortation to the believers to fight the unbelieving kings without fear, since God exalts whom He wills and humbles whom He wills. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di read it rather as an affirmation that the One who governs the universe will not leave His servants misguided without clarification of what concerns them. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that its purpose is to show that God alone is the protector and the helper, so that believers turn to Him alone and disown everything else. Al-Razi offers several readings: the one who holds sovereignty can defend the believers even when they are separated from unbelieving relatives. The commentators also discuss how the verse connects with the preceding passages on seeking forgiveness for polytheists. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya record the debate about divine misguidance: the Mu'tazilites understand that God punishes no one before informing them, a view the Sunni scholars do not share in the same way. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy find the same principle but add that a believer who transgresses after being informed of a prohibition falls under misguidance. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the mention of sovereignty and the power over life and death reinforces God's perfect knowledge. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi note that the surah's closing themes of divine protection serve as comfort for the believers.

This verse says that God turned in mercy towards the Prophet ﷺ and the Emigrants and Helpers who followed him in the expedition of Tabuk, called the hour of hardship because of the scorching heat, scarcity of mounts, water and provisions, when ten men shared a camel and two men shared one date. The commentators give the word repentance related meanings. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi see it as pardon for the permission given to the hypocrites to stay behind, or as deliverance from hardship; al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi stress a favour preceding the fault and then a second pardon; al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read it as a general reminder that every believer, even the prophets, needs repentance. On the phrase that the hearts of a group nearly swerved, most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand a leaning towards staying behind or turning back, not apostasy; al-Mawardi cites Ibn Abbas on a withdrawal from support for the Prophet, and al-Hasan speaks of a group wanting to turn back. They agree that this inclination never became action and only came close. Commentators differ on the repetition of repentance: some take it as emphasis, others as an initial favour before the sin and a second acceptance after it. Several report the account of Abu Bakr's prayer and the rain that followed. All conclude that God is compassionate and merciful towards them, with some saying ra'fa means removing harm and rahma means bestowing benefit.

This verse recalls that God turned in forgiveness toward the three men who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya and Mararah ibn al-Rabi'. Commentators differ on the meaning of 'were left behind' (khullifu). Mujahid, Abu Malik and Ibn 'Abbas take it to mean that their repentance was deferred, as happened to Abu Lubaba and his companions; Qatada takes it to mean that they stayed behind from the campaign. Ka'b ibn Malik himself rejected the latter reading and explained that it meant their excuse was not accepted, not their absence from the fighting. The phrase 'the earth became constricted for them despite its vastness' conveys the distress and isolation they felt, when the Muslims shunned them for fifty nights and they were told to keep away from their wives. They concluded that there was no refuge from God except in Him, that is, in seeking His forgiveness. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate Ka'b's account at length, while al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi note that the repetition of the pardon is for emphasis. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Qayyim explain that 'so that they might repent' means that they should persevere in repentance. All agree that God is the Accepter of Repentance, the Most Merciful, and that the trial served as expiation and as a lesson for the believers.

This verse commands believers to fear God, meaning to obey Him and avoid what He forbids, and to be with the truthful. The commentators agree that truthfulness here covers sincerity of intention, speech and action, but they differ on who the truthful are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy report, through Nafi' and al-Dahhak, that they are the Prophet and his companions, with al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr naming Abu Bakr and Umar. Ibn 'Abbas is cited by al-Tha'labi and al-Sam'ani as meaning those whose intentions were pure and who went with the Prophet to Tabuk. Ibn Jurayj identifies them as the emigrants, citing Surat al-Hashr, while al-Suddi takes them to be the three men who stayed behind and honestly admitted their fault, and Qatada reads it as a general rule for anyone truthful in word, intention and deed. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Shawkani understand it as those faithful to their faith and their covenant with God and His Messenger.

Ibn Mas'ud read it as «among the truthful» and explained it as truthfulness of speech, saying that lying is unfitting in earnest or in jest. Al-Tabari, who holds the common reading «with», finds Ibn Mas'ud's interpretation sound in meaning. Most commentators report that the verse was revealed in the story of the three men who stayed behind from Tabuk, although Ibn al-Jawzi notes an opinion that it concerns People of the Book who believed. Al-Razi draws from it that consensus is a proof and that truthfulness is a great virtue, a point al-Qurtubi also makes, adding that a liar's testimony and authority are invalid.

It was not fitting for the people of Medina or the Bedouins around them to stay behind when the Messenger of God set out to fight, nor to value their own selves above his. The verse takes the form of a statement but carries the force of a prohibition. It explains that whoever endures thirst, weariness, or hunger in God's cause, or treads a ground that enrages the unbelievers, or inflicts any harm on the enemy, has a righteous deed recorded for him, for God does not waste the reward of the good-doers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand these hardships as meritorious in themselves, and al-Zamakhshari stresses that believers should share the Prophet's dangers with eagerness and willing hearts. The commentators agree that even ordinary acts such as walking, speaking, or spending are rewarded when done with a sincere intention, as al-Razi and al-Nasafi explain. They disagree on how far the ruling extends. Qatada and those who followed him, including al-Wahidi and al-Qurtubi, say it is specific to the Prophet leaving in person, while other rulers may be followed only when needed. Ibn Zayd holds that it was abrogated by the verse saying the believers should not all go forth together, since Islam was then small in number. Al-Tabari rejects abrogation and sees no contradiction between the two verses. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi hold that the ruling applies to those the leader has specifically summoned to march.

This verse teaches that believers who march with the Prophet ﷺ on campaign are credited for everything they endure: thirst, weariness, hunger, every step that enrages the disbelievers, and every gain taken from the enemy. Every expense, small or great, and every valley they cross, is written for them as a good deed, so that God may reward them with the best of what they did. The commentators agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Qatada and others understood the valley as any stretch of land crossed, and the small expense as anything as slight as a date or the strap of a whip. They support this with hadiths on spending in God's cause. On the phrase 'the best of what they did', al-Razi and al-Baydawi offer two readings: God rewards obligatory and recommended acts but not merely permitted ones, or the reward itself is better than the deeds. Abu Hayyan finds the second reading more coherent. Ibn Kathir also cites the generous spending of Uthman during the army of hardship. The following verse raises the question of whether all must go out together. Al-Tabari, following al-Hasan, holds that a group should go out while another remains to learn the religion and later teach those who return. Ibn Abbas, in one report, takes the passage as referring to hypocrites. Qatada and Ibn Zayd consider the ruling abrogated, while al-Awza'i and others regard it as valid for all times.

This verse teaches that believers should not all set out together for battle, but that a group from each community should go forth while another group stays with the Prophet ﷺ to gain understanding of the religion, and then warn their people when they return. The commentators differ on the meaning of the going forth and on whom the pronouns in "that they may gain understanding" and "that they may warn" refer to. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak, as reported by al-Tabari, hold that the verse concerns the detachments sent out by the Prophet, the group remaining in Medina being the one that learns. Al-Hasan, followed by al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi, holds instead that the understanding and the warning belong to the group that goes out. Several scholars, including al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur, note that the verse sets out a division of duties between fighters and scholars. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi draw from it that seeking knowledge is a collective obligation, and see in it evidence that a single reporter's testimony is valid, a view al-Qadi disputes according to al-Razi. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi report several occasions of revelation, notably the reply to hypocrites who said that the Bedouins who stayed behind were lost. Ibn Qayyim presents both readings and favours the first as best fitting the context of fighting. Al-Zamakhshari stresses that the aim of knowledge is warning and guidance rather than status.

This verse commands the believers to fight the disbelievers who live near them, beginning with the nearest in dwelling and kinship, and to show toughness, courage and steadfastness against them. The commentators agree on the principle of priority by proximity, on the meaning of ghilzah as harshness, bravery and endurance in battle, and on the promise that God is with the pious. They differ, however, on who the "nearby" disbelievers are. Ibn Umar says they were the Byzantines, who held Syria, closer to Medina than Iraq; al-Hasan names the Daylam; Ibn Abbas names the Jewish tribes of Qurayza, al-Nadir, Khaybar and Fadak; and Ibn Zayd says they were the Arabs, before the later command to fight the People of the Book. Qatada reads the verse in general terms: fight the nearest, then the next nearest. Al-Hasan considered it abrogated by the command to fight the polytheists collectively, but al-Razi and the scholars who follow him reject abrogation, holding that starting with the nearest is the best way to carry out the general command. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir stress that harshness is not meant to be a permanent trait: believers should be gentle with one another and firm against the enemy. Al-Tabari concludes that each region is obliged to fight its nearest enemies unless another region needs its help.

This passage describes how the hypocrites reacted when a surah was revealed. Some of them asked one another, mockingly and dismissively, which of them this surah had increased in faith. God replies that it increases the faith of those who believe, who rejoice at it, while it adds filth to the filth of those in whose hearts is a sickness, meaning doubt and hypocrisy, so that they die as disbelievers. The commentators generally agree that the verses concern the hypocrites. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the increase in faith as a new, specific assurance regarding the rulings, reports and proofs the surah contains, and they hold that faith grows and diminishes. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya add that the growth of action is also an increase in faith. Ibn 'Atiyya explains several ways in which revelation strengthens conviction. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi take rijs to mean doubt, Muqatil takes it to mean sin, and al-Zajjaj and Qutrub take it to mean disbelief. Opinions also differ on the trial that befalls them yearly. Mujahid mentions famine, Qatada and al-Hasan mention fighting, Hudhayfa mentions lying, Ikrima mentions alternating between hypocrisy and faith, and Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as God exposing their secrets. The verses also describe how they slip away when the surah is recited, and God turns their hearts because they do not understand.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the hypocrites whose hearts harbour a sickness, meaning doubt and hypocrisy. When a surah is revealed, it adds to their existing filth, rijs, and they die in disbelief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi largely agree that they reject each new surah, so their disbelief grows with each one. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that rijs here means disbelief, doubt or sin, following the explanations attributed to Qatada, Ibn Abbas and Muqatil.

Al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Qayyim explain why the increase is attributed to the surah itself: it is the occasion that exposes and deepens their rejection, while believers gain faith from it. Ibn al-Qayyim adds that guidance and misguidance are acts of God, whereas disbelief is the act of people, and he criticises the Qadariyya and Jabriyya on this point. Al-Razi argues that the surah may strengthen worldly attachment in some hearts, pushing them further from faith.

The meaning of fitna in the phrase "tested once or twice every year" is disputed. Mujahid and Ibn Atiyya take it as hunger and sickness, al-Hasan and Qatada as being summoned to fight, Hudhayfa as lies, and al-Zamakhshari as various trials sent by God. Ibn Atiyya considers it more likely that God exposes their secrets, while al-Alusi simply reports the various views without deciding between them.

In this verse God asks the hypocrites whether they do not see that they are tested once or twice every year, yet they neither repent nor take heed. The commentators differ on what this trial is. Mujahid, Ata' and Ibn Kathir report it as drought and famine, or as sickness and pain, while al-Dahhak takes it as high prices and the withholding of rain. Qatada and al-Hasan understand it as campaigns of fighting alongside the Prophet, where they witness God's promise of victory fulfilled. Ibn Kathir also reports that Hudhayfa explained it as the lies the polytheists spread about the Prophet, while Muqatil ibn Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as the exposure of the hypocrites' inner secrets, and Ibn 'Atiyya prefers this view because it fits the context before and after the verse. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi mention several meanings, and al-Zamakhshari adds that Satan may mislead them into breaking their covenants. Al-Tabari holds that no report decides between these views, so it is best to keep to the plain wording of the verse. Most commentators agree that it rebukes them for persisting in hypocrisy. In recitation, Hamza and Ya'qub read the verb in the second person, addressing the believers, the majority read it in the third person about the hypocrites, and Ibn Mas'ud reads it addressed to the Prophet.

This verse describes how the hypocrites behaved when a surah was revealed that exposed their faults. They exchanged glances and signals, out of mockery or anger, and asked whether any believer could see them. If no one was watching they slipped away, and if someone was, they stayed put. Afterwards they withdrew from the place of revelation for fear of exposure. The commentators agree that the people meant are the hypocrites. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud read the glance as a wordless sign, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan also see it as an expression of surprise or derision. The next clause, that God turned their hearts away, can be taken as a report or as a curse, and al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi note both readings. Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi understand it as a consequence imposed on them for their conduct. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur stress that God alone turns hearts. Al-Razi argues from the necessity of a cause that comes from God, and he answers Mu'tazili objections that such turning cannot be a punishment. Several authors, among them al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, cite a saying of Ibn 'Abbas advising against saying "we have left the prayer", which Ibn Juzayy and al-Jaza'iri connect with good manners in speech. The phrase "people who do not understand" is generally taken to mean failing to reflect in a way that leads to faith.

This verse reminds the Arabs of God's favour in sending them a messenger from among themselves, of their own lineage, language and kin, whose integrity they know. The commentators agree that "ʿazīzun ʿalayhi mā ʿanittum" means that what distresses them distresses him, and that "ḥarīṣun ʿalaykum" expresses his eagerness for their guidance and welfare, while "bil-mu'minīna raʾūfun raḥīm" is directed at the believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Ibn ʿAbbas, read "ʿanittum" as their going astray or their sin, whereas Qatada took it to mean the hardship of their believers; al-Tabari preferred Ibn ʿAbbas's view because the wording is general. Al-Razi notes that compassion is attributed only to believers, since the Prophet is firm with disbelievers. Regarding the reading "min anfusikum" with a fatha, Ibn ʿAbbas and others read it as "from among the noblest of you", and Ibn ʿAbbas said every Arab tribe had produced one of the Prophet's ancestors, a view cited by al-Qurtubi and Ibn ʿAtiyya. Most commentators take the address to be to the Arabs, while al-Zajjaj takes it to be all mankind. Some transmit from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that these two verses were among the last revealed, a claim other scholars examine. The verse teaches the believer to rely on God when people turn away.

In the closing verses of Surah al-Tawba, God reminds the Arabs of His favour in sending them a messenger from among themselves, of their own kind, language and lineage, whose uprightness they know. The commentators agree that what grieves the Prophet is the hardship his people suffer, and that he is eager for their guidance, compassionate and merciful toward the believers. God then instructs him, should they turn away, to say: 'God is sufficient for me', meaning that He suffices for all that concerns him, that there is no god but Him, that he has placed his trust in Him and relies upon Him, the Lord of the mighty Throne. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that the turning away refers to the disbelievers and hypocrites. On the meaning of turning away, al-Hasan takes it as turning from obedience to God, while Ali ibn Isa takes it as turning from the Prophet himself; al-Razi also mentions refusing the demanding duties or abandoning support for the struggle. The commentators largely agree that these two verses were among the last revealed, according to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, though some attach that report to another verse. The Throne is singled out, according to al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi, for its greatness and vastness. Ibn Muhaysin's reading, 'al-'azimu' in the nominative, makes the epithet describe the Lord, whereas the common reading attaches it to the Throne.
